# Chakravyuha — An Active Directory Purple Team Lab

[![Chakravyuha Project Website](https://img.shields.io/badge/Project-chakravyuha.tech-blue?style=flat-square)](https://chakravyuha.tech)
[![MIT License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green?style=flat-square)](LICENSE)
[![MITRE ATT&CK](https://img.shields.io/badge/ATT%26CK-T1558.003-red?style=flat-square)](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/)
[![MITRE Engage](https://img.shields.io/badge/Engage-EAC0002-orange?style=flat-square)](docs/engage-mapping.md)

A purple-team Active Directory lab proving offense, defense, and architecture together — not just an attack showcase. Every technique follows **Attack → Detect → Respond → Harden**, integrated with a built-in deception layer, custom Sigma/Wazuh detection rules written from scratch, and enterprise remediation via Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA).

**Project Website & Technical Deep-Dives:** [https://chakravyuha.tech](https://chakravyuha.tech)  
**Status:** Module 1 (Kerberoasting) is **Complete & Verified** — attack execution, Event 4769 RC4 detection, honeypot SPN alerts, and gMSA remediation are fully validated in the lab and documented end-to-end. Modules 2–9 are scheduled across the attack chain.

---

## What This Is

CTFs and pre-configured labs typically teach you how to run an exploit tool, grab a flag, and move on. They rarely expose you to the messy reality of Windows security logging, event parsing, SIEM pipeline bottlenecks, or the defensive engineering required to permanently eliminate an attack surface.

Chakravyuha was built from bare metal up to bridge that gap. It is an enterprise-style Active Directory environment (`CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL`) running across an isolated host-only network. It features a Windows Server 2022 Domain Controller, a Windows Server 2019 member server, Windows 10 client workstations, a strict three-tier administrative model, an active deception surface (honey SPNs, canary credentials), and an Ubuntu-based Wazuh SIEM pipeline. 

The lab's purpose is to execute nine fundamental AD attack techniques in sequence, analyze the exact Windows telemetry generated by each, build production-grade detections, and implement durable architectural hardening.

---

## Lab Architecture

![Chakravyuha lab architecture diagram](docs/images/architecture.png)

```
CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL — 192.168.10.0/24 (Host-Only Virtual Network)

DC-01 (.10, Server 2022, DC + DNS + KDC) ──── SRV-01 (.20, Server 2019, File + IIS)
  • Active Directory Domain Services            • Tier 1 Resource Server
  • Kerberos Key Distribution Center            • gmsa.sqlsvc (gMSA, 120-char auto-rotated password)
  • Native Wazuh Agent forwarding Security logs  • svc.sqlsvc (Legacy account, SPN retired, AES-only)
                                                • svc.sqlreport (Decoy SPN, Deception Honey Account)
       │                                              │
       ├──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
       │                      │
  WS-01 (.30, Win10 Ent)   WS-02 (.31, Win10 Ent)
  • Tier 2 / Finance OU    • Tier 2 / Engineering OU
  • User: pnair            • User: rdesai
  • Managed via adm.t2     • Managed via adm.t2
       │                      │
       └──────────────┬───────┘
                      │
               Virtual Switch (192.168.10.0/24)
                      │
             SIEM (.50, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS)
             • Wazuh Manager v4.x + OpenSearch Backend
             • Real-time alerting for Security Event IDs 4769, 4768, 4624, 4662

KALI (.100, Host-Only + NAT) — Dedicated attack platform with isolated host-only lab access
```

Comprehensive architecture details, network layout, and tiering boundaries: [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md)

---

## Attack & Defense Modules

| # | Technique | ATT&CK ID | Key Telemetry | Lab Status | Documentation & Deep-Dive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | **Kerberoasting** | T1558.003 | Security 4769 (RC4 `0x17`) | **Complete** | [`Module 1 Guide`](modules/01-kerberoasting/README.md) · [Deep-Dive Post](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-4-kerberoasting-attack) |
| 02 | **AS-REP Roasting** | T1558.004 | Security 4768 (No Pre-Auth) | Planned | Scheduled |
| 03 | **Pass-the-Hash** | T1550.002 | Security 4624 (Logon Type 3, NTLM) | Planned | Scheduled |
| 04 | **Pass-the-Ticket / Silver Ticket** | T1558.002 | Security 4769 / 4768 | Planned | Scheduled |
| 05 | **Golden Ticket** | T1558.001 | Security 4769 (Abnormal KRBTGT Lifetime) | Planned | Scheduled |
| 06 | **DCSync** | T1003.006 | Security 4662 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) | Planned | Scheduled |
| 07 | **BloodHound ACL Abuse** | T1078.002 | Security 4728 / 4732 / 5136 | Planned | Scheduled |
| 08 | **LAPS Bypass** | T1555 | Security 4662 / Directory Read | Planned | Scheduled |
| 09 | **AD CS ESC1** | T1649 | Certification Authority 4886 / 4887 | Planned | Scheduled |

Every module follows a rigorous 8-section engineering framework: **Executive Summary → Technical Theory & Lab Setup → Attack Execution → Detection Engineering → Defensive Response & Triaging → Remediation & Hardening → ATT&CK & Engage Mapping → Verification & Lessons Learned**.

---

## Core Engineering Principles

- **Deception Layer Built-in from Day One:** Decoy service accounts (`svc.sqlreport`), fake SPNs (`MSSQLsSvc/SQLPROD01`), and planted bait artifacts (`IT_credentials_backup.pdf` on WS-01, `employees.csv` on DC-01) sit alongside production assets. Attackers scanning or requesting tickets for lure accounts trigger zero-false-positive alerts before touching production data. See [`deception/README.md`](deception/README.md) and [`docs/engage-mapping.md`](docs/engage-mapping.md).
- **First-Principles Detection Engineering:** Detection rules are not copied from vendor bundles; they are written by analyzing raw Windows event structures (`EventID 4769`, `TicketEncryptionType: 0x17`, `ServiceName`). Every rule includes both Sigma format for cross-platform portability and native Wazuh XML definitions. See [`detections/README.md`](detections/README.md).
- **Enterprise-Grade Remediation:** Rather than applying temporary mitigations, root causes are fixed using modern Active Directory primitives. For service account abuse, traditional accounts are migrated to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) featuring 120-character auto-rotated cryptographically secure passwords and Kerberos AES256 enforcement. See [`hardening/README.md`](hardening/README.md).
- **Strict Three-Tier Administration:** Tier 0 (`adm.t0.yash`), Tier 1 (`adm.t1.yash`), and Tier 2 (`adm.t2.yash`) credentials never cross tier boundaries, preventing credential dumping and lateral traversal across the domain. See [`decisions.md`](decisions.md).

---

## Published Engineering Deep-Dives

Detailed architectural logs and technical breakdowns published at [chakravyuha.tech](https://chakravyuha.tech):

- **[Post 0: Architecture & Design Decisions](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-0-architecture)** — Threat modeling, sizing constraints, 3-tier administrative segmentation, and why a custom domain was built over canned templates.
- **[Post 1: Lab Build & Active Directory Deployment](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-1-lab-build)** — Deploying Windows Server 2022/2019, domain configuration, automated user provisioning, DNS debugging, and GPO troubleshooting.
- **[Post 2: Detection Pipeline & Log Engineering](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-2-log-pipeline)** — Advanced audit policy configuration, native Wazuh agent telemetry forwarding, resolving OpenSearch disk-full index write locks, and pipeline validation.
- **[Post 3: Attack Execution: Kerberoasting Deep Dive](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-3-kerberoasting)** — Kerberos TGS protocol mechanics, SPN harvesting, RC4 downgrade ticket requests, offline hash extraction, and cracking analysis.
- **[Post 4: Hardening: gMSA Migration & AES Enforcement](https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/posts/post-4-hardening)** — Retiring legacy SPNs, KDS root key deployment, provisioning gMSA (`gmsa.sqlsvc`) with 120-character auto-rotating passwords, and Kerberos AES256 enforcement.

---

## Repository Structure

```

├── README.md                           # Main lab landing page and overview
├── LICENSE                             # MIT license
├── .gitignore                          # Security and build exclusions
├── decisions.md                        # Architectural and engineering decisions log
├── configs/                            # Sysmon, audit policy, and agent configurations
├── deception/                          # Deception layer architecture and decoys
│   └── README.md                       # Deception strategy, honeypots, and canary tokens
├── detections/                         # Detection engineering rules and catalog
│   ├── README.md                       # Detection catalog and rule mapping
│   ├── sigma/                          # Sigma detection rules
│   │   └── kerberoasting_rc4_4769.yml  # Event 4769 RC4 ticket detection
│   └── wazuh/                          # Wazuh rules and decoders
│       └── local_rules.xml             # Custom rules (100101, 100102)
├── docs/                               # Architectural and implementation documentation
│   ├── architecture.md                 # Network topology, hosts, and tiered admin model
│   ├── lab-build.md                    # Lab deployment log and troubleshooting
│   ├── log-pipeline.md                 # Log forwarding and Wazuh pipeline engineering
│   ├── attack-readiness-gate.md        # Pre-attack verification checklist
│   ├── engage-mapping.md               # MITRE Engage deception matrix mapping
│   └── images/                         # Architectural diagrams and schematics
│       └── architecture.png            # Network and identity topology diagram
├── hardening/                          # Remediation, gMSA migration, and GPO policies
│   └── README.md                       # Hardening strategy and implementation details
├── modules/                            # Attack execution and purple-team modules
│   └── 01-kerberoasting/               # Module 1: Kerberoasting attack and defense
│       ├── README.md                   # Comprehensive 8-section purple-team guide
│       └── evidence/                   # Sanitized logs, tickets, and execution artifacts
└── scripts/                            # Automation, deployment, and validation scripts
```

---

## Author & Contact

**Yash Gulati**  
*Aspiring SOC Analyst (L1) / Application Security Engineer*  
- **Project Site:** [https://chakravyuha.tech](https://chakravyuha.tech)  
- **Personal Portfolio:** [https://yashgulati.tech](https://yashgulati.tech)  
- **LinkedIn:** [https://www.linkedin.com/in/yashgulatii/](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yashgulatii/)  

---

## Disclaimer

This project is developed solely for authorized defensive research, detection engineering, and educational purple teaming within a strictly isolated, host-only laboratory environment. It does not target, interact with, or represent any production system or infrastructure.

architecture.content:
# Lab Architecture

![img](../docs/images/architecture.png)

## Network

```
CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL — 192.168.10.0/24 (Host-Only)

DC-01 (.10, Srv2022, DC+DNS+KDC) ── SRV-01 (.20, Srv2019, File+IIS,
  svc.sqlsvc [SPN retired] + gmsa.sqlsvc [real SPN, gMSA] + svc.sqlreport, SPNs)
       │                                    │
  WS-01 (.30, Win10, Tier2\Finance,    WS-02 (.31, Win10, Tier2\Engineering,
  pnair, admin via IT-Support)          rdesai, admin via IT-Support)
       │                                    │
       └──────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                  Virtual Switch
                       │
              SIEM (.50, Ubuntu, Wazuh)

KALI (.100, Host-Only + NAT) — attack platform, controlled internet egress only
```

Two VMware virtual networks are in play: **Host-Only** (`192.168.10.0/24`), which carries all lab/domain traffic, and **NAT**, used only by Kali for tool updates. Every domain-joined machine's IP is pinned at the VMware network console level — not just inside the guest OS — specifically because having both adapters active on a VM led to it answering on whichever network it felt like at boot, which briefly broke DNS resolution for the domain during the build (see `lab-build.md`).

## Hosts

| Host | IP | OS | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| DC-01 | `.10` | Windows Server 2022 | Domain Controller — AD DS, DNS, KDC |
| SRV-01 | `.20` | Windows Server 2019 | File Server + IIS, hosts the SPN-bearing service accounts |
| WS-01 | `.30` | Windows 10 Enterprise | Tier 2 / Finance workstation, daily user `pnair` |
| WS-02 | `.31` | Windows 10 Enterprise | Tier 2 / Engineering workstation, daily user `rdesai` |
| SIEM | `.50` | Ubuntu 22.04 | Wazuh manager — log aggregation and detection |
| KALI | `.100` | Kali Linux | Attack platform — Host-Only for lab traffic, NAT for tool updates only |

## Tiered Administrative Model

The lab enforces Microsoft's AD Tiering Model as actual access control, not just a diagram:

| Tier | Account | Scope | Group |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `adm.t0.yash` | DC-01 only, ever | Domain Admins |
| 1 | `adm.t1.yash` | SRV-01 only, ever | `Tier1-Server-Admins` (local admin grant on SRV-01) |
| 2 | `adm.t2.yash` | WS-01/WS-02 only | `IT-Support` (local admin via GPO Restricted Groups on the Tier 2 OU) |

The rule that's never broken: no tiered admin credential is ever used outside its own tier. A Tier 0 credential typed into a Tier 2 workstation is only as safe as that workstation's security — the whole point of the tiering model is to stop a single compromised machine from cascading into full domain compromise.

One deliberate exception sits inside this design: `IT-Support` has local admin on both WS-01 and WS-02, while the daily-use accounts (`pnair`, `rdesai`) do not. That gap — "I'm not local admin, but a group I'm not a member of is" — is a planted BloodHound lateral-movement path, left alone until Module 7 (BloodHound ACL Abuse).

## Logging

Each of DC-01, SRV-01, WS-01, and WS-02 runs its own native Wazuh agent (no centralized WEF/WEC collector in this lab). See `log-pipeline.md` for the pipeline's actual verification history, including a real failure found during setup.

lab-build.title: Lab Build
lab-build.content:
# Lab Build

## Sequence

1. **VMware Workstation Pro** installed; two virtual networks created — NAT (internet) and Host-Only (`192.168.10.0/24`, isolated lab traffic).
2. **DC-01** built first (Windows Server 2022): static IP `192.168.10.10`, promoted to Domain Controller, domain `CORP.CHAKRAVYUH.LOCAL` created.
3. **SRV-01** built (Windows Server 2019): joined the domain, static IP `.20`, File Server role installed, SPN registered on `svc.sqlsvc`.
4. **WS-01** and **WS-02** built (Windows 10 Enterprise): joined the domain, static IPs `.30`/`.31`, placed in separate Tier 2 sub-OUs (Finance / Engineering).
5. **SIEM** built (Ubuntu 22.04): Wazuh installed, agents deployed to all four Windows hosts.
6. **KALI** built and networked: Host-Only for lab traffic, NAT for tool updates only.
7. **Realism pass:** full OU hierarchy built around the AD Tiering Model (not flat), filler/employee accounts added with varied placement, GPO baseline configured (Default Domain Policy + `Workstation-Baseline-Restrictions`), Sysmon deployed to all Windows hosts.

## Real issues hit during the build

The build wasn't frictionless, and the friction turned out to be informative rather than just annoying.

**DNS / networking conflict.** With both NAT and Host-Only adapters active, DC-01 ended up reachable over whichever network actually answered — querying its intended static IP (`192.168.10.10`) from another device returned nothing, while the NAT adapter's IP, which changed on every reboot, was the one actually responding. Nothing about Kerberos or AD DS was broken; the domain simply wasn't reachable at the address everything expected. The fix was applied at the **VMware network console level** — setting each machine's static IP as the default directly in VMware's network settings — rather than fighting adapter priority inside the guest OS.

**GPO scope learned the hard way.** A `Workstation-Baseline-Restrictions` GPO was set up restricting logon to specific workstations, linked to the Tier 2 OU. Testing it by RDPing into a WS-02 shortly after resulted in being locked out of that machine — a direct, first-hand lesson that linking a GPO to an OU applies exactly what's configured, precisely, not loosely.

**Tiered admin model — confusion before it clicked.** Setting up separate Tier 0/1/2 admin identities, each scoped to its own tier, was conceptually unclear at first — not a single failure, but genuine uncertainty about why three separate admin accounts mattered more than one admin account used everywhere. The reasoning clicked once it was clear a Tier 0 credential typed on a Tier 2 machine is only as safe as that machine's own security.

**Power cuts and snapshot discipline.** Local power cuts corrupted VM state more than once during the build. Snapshotting before any risky change went from "best practice read about" to a habit actually relied on.

## Pre-lab study

Six stages of self-directed study ran in parallel with the build: Windows Fundamentals, Active Directory Deep Understanding, Windows Authentication & Credential Storage, SPNs Deep Dive, Detection & SIEM Foundations, and Virtualization & Lab Networking. Two external resources were genuinely useful for the Kerberos/AD conceptual pieces specifically and are credited in Blog Post #2.

log-pipeline.title: Log Pipeline
log-pipeline.content:
# Log Pipeline

## Setup

Each of DC-01, SRV-01, WS-01, and WS-02 runs its own native Wazuh agent, reporting to a single Wazuh manager on the SIEM host (`192.168.10.50`, Ubuntu 22.04). There's no centralized Windows Event Forwarding/WEC collector in this design — each host ships its own logs directly. Sysmon is deployed on all four Windows hosts to extend native Windows logging with process, network, and registry telemetry, which is what makes writing meaningful Sigma rules possible in the first place.

## Verification, not assumption

A pipeline that's "configured" and a pipeline that's "confirmed working" are different claims, and this lab treats the difference as load-bearing: no attack module runs until the logging pipeline is verified end-to-end, not just installed (see the Attack Readiness Gate in the project's working notes).

That verification caught a real problem early on. Test events (deliberate failed logons, generated per host) weren't reaching Wazuh's Discover view — not because the agents weren't sending them, but because the SIEM manager's root disk had filled up with old `wazuh-archives-*` indices. That pushed OpenSearch into a `create_index` block, which silently broke Filebeat's ability to publish new archives. Events were reaching the manager fine; they just weren't landing anywhere visible. Clearing the old indices and confirming test events reappeared in Discover closed the gap.

This is exactly the kind of failure a real SOC pipeline can hit — a log source that looks fine at a glance but is quietly failing downstream — and it's part of why "detection confirmed firing" means something concrete in this project's module write-ups: each module's Sigma rule is verified against a pipeline that's been independently checked, not assumed to be working.

## Baseline

Before any attack module ran, the lab was left running for a period to observe what "normal" log volume and logon activity actually looks like — without that baseline, attack-generated noise is hard to distinguish from ordinary domain activity.

attack-readiness-gate.content:
# Attack Readiness Gate

This document defines the pre-attack verification checklist that must pass before executing any purple team module in the Chakravyuha lab. The gate ensures telemetry integrity, detection efficacy, and environmental consistency.

## Gate Philosophy

> **"No attack executes without verified telemetry."**
> 
> Every module must prove its detection logic works against a known-good attack before the module is considered complete. This gate is the quality control checkpoint.

---

## 4-Point Verification Checklist

### 1. Telemetry Pipeline Integrity

**Objective:** Confirm Windows Security events flow from endpoints → SIEM → Wazuh → OpenSearch without loss.

| Check | Command / Verification | Pass Criteria |
|-------|------------------------|---------------|
| **1.1** Wazuh agent connected on all endpoints | `/var/ossec/bin/agent_control -l` on SIEM | All 5 agents (DC-01, SRV-01, WS-01, WS-02, Kali) show `Active` status |
| **1.2** Event ID 4769 generated on DC for test SPN request | `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4769} -MaxEvents 1` on DC-01 | Event present with `TicketEncryptionType` field populated |

# MITRE Engage Deception Activity Mapping

This document maps each Chakravyuha lab module to its corresponding ATT&CK technique and MITRE Engage deception activity. The mapping is based on [MITRE Engage](https://engage.mitre.org/) activity definitions and is used to justify the deception infrastructure deployed in the lab.

## Mapping Table

> **Disclaimer:** Module 01's deception asset (`svc.sqlreport`) is deployed and verified, though not before Module 1 ran — see decisions.md. The deception assets listed for Modules 02-09 below are planned design intent and have not been built yet.

| Module | ATT&CK Technique | Technique Name | Engage Activity ID | Engage Activity Name | Deception Asset Deployed | Operational Goal |
|--------|------------------|----------------|--------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|------------------|
| 01 | T1558.003 | Kerberoasting | EAC0002 | **Credential** | `svc.sqlreport` with honey SPN `MSSQLsSvc/SQLPROD01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433` | Lure attacker into requesting ticket for fake SQL service; detect via Rule 100102 |
| 02 | T1558.004 | AS-REP Roasting | EAC0002 | **Credential** | `svc.asrep` (no pre-auth required) | Detect AS-REQ for accounts without pre-auth |
| 03 | T1550.002 | Pass-the-Hash | EAC0004 | **Session** | Honey share `\\SRV-01\IT_Backups` with planted NTLM hash artifact | Trigger PtH attempt; alert on anomalous Logon Type 3 from Kali IP |
| 04 | T1558.002 | Silver Ticket | EAC0004 | **Session** | Exported ticket for `svc.sqlreport` planted on WS-01 desktop | Detect ticket reuse from unauthorized host |
| 05 | T1558.001 | Golden Ticket | EAC0003 | **Identity** | Fake `krbtgt` hash planted in `IT_credentials_backup.pdf` | Detect forged tickets with abnormal lifetime/end-time |
| 06 | T1003.006 | DCSync | EAC0001 | **Data** | Deception OU with fake privileged accounts | Detect Directory Replication requests from non-DC |
| 07 | T1078.002 | BloodHound ACL Abuse | EAC0005 | **Privilege** | Over-permissive ACLs on `CN=Deception_Admins,OU=IT` | Detect ACL enumeration and abuse chains |
| 08 | T1555 | LAPS Bypass | EAC0006 | **Local Account** | Fake LAPS password in `C:\IT$\Scripts\laps-backup.ps1` | Detect unauthorized LAPS reads |
| 09 | T1649 | AD CS ESC1 | EAC0007 | **Certificate** | Vulnerable template `Chakravyuha_User` with `Enrollee Supplies Subject` | Detect certificate request abuse |

## Engage Activity Definitions (from engage.mitre.org)

### EAC0001 - Data
> **Objective:** Expose adversary to synthetic or modified data.
> **Application:** Plant false credentials, documents, or configuration files that lead adversaries toward monitored systems.

### EAC0002 - Credential
> **Objective:** Expose adversary to synthetic or modified credentials.
> **Application:** Create honey accounts, service accounts with SPNs, or planted credentials that trigger alerts when used.

### EAC0003 - Identity
> **Objective:** Expose adversary to synthetic or modified identities.
> **Application:** Create fake user/service accounts with attractive privileges or group memberships.

### EAC0004 - Session
> **Objective:** Expose adversary to synthetic or modified sessions.
> **Application:** Plant session artifacts (tickets, tokens, hashes) that can be reused and monitored.

### EAC0005 - Privilege
> **Objective:** Expose adversary to synthetic or modified privileges.
> **Application:** Create over-privileged accounts or misconfigured ACLs that attract privilege escalation attempts.

### EAC0006 - Local Account
> **Objective:** Expose adversary to synthetic or modified local accounts.
> **Application:** Plant local administrator credentials or LAPS-managed passwords in accessible locations.

### EAC0007 - Certificate
> **Objective:** Expose adversary to synthetic or modified certificates.
> **Application:** Configure vulnerable certificate templates or plant PFX files for certificate abuse detection.

## Deception Architecture in Chakravyuha

### Network Placement
- **SIEM (192.168.10.50):** Central log collection, Wazuh rule evaluation
- **DC-01 (192.168.10.10):** AD DS, KDC, SPN registration for honey accounts
- **SRV-01 (192.168.10.20):** File server hosting honey shares and planted documents
- **WS-01 (192.168.10.30):** Endpoint with planted artifacts (desktop, C:\IT$)
- **WS-02 (192.168.10.31):** Clean endpoint for baseline comparison
- **Kali (192.168.10.100):** Attacker perspective; source of all adversarial telemetry

### Deception Credential Inventory

| Account | Type | Password/Secret | Location Planted | Engage Activity |
|---------|------|-----------------|------------------|-----------------|
| `svc.sqlsvc` | Service (vulnerable) | `<redacted>` | SPN registered on DC | — (Target for remediation) |
| `gmsa.sqlsvc` | gMSA (remediated) | Auto-rotated 120-char | SPN migrated from svc.sqlsvc | — (Defense) |
| `svc.sqlreport` | Service (honey) | `<redacted>` | Honey SPN on DC (created 2026-10-23) | EAC0002 - Credential |
| `svc.asrep` | User (honey) | No pre-auth required | AD Users & Computers | EAC0002 - Credential |
| `krbtgt_fake` | Identity (fake) | N/A | `IT_credentials_backup.pdf` on WS-01 (2026-07-01) | EAC0003 - Identity |
| `employees.csv` | Filler/bait | Canary token (CSV) | `C:\Users\Administrator\employees.csv` on DC-01 (2026-06-28) | EAC0001 - Data |

### Detection-to-Deception Traceability

Each Wazuh rule maps to a specific deception asset:

| Wazuh Rule | Deception Asset | Engage Activity | Alert Meaning |
|------------|-----------------|-----------------|---------------|
| 100102 | `svc.sqlreport` SPN | EAC0002 | Attacker requested RC4 ticket for honey SPN from Kali |
| (Module 02) | `svc.asrep` | EAC0002 | AS-REQ without pre-auth for honey account |
| (Module 03) | Planted NTLM hash artifact | EAC0004 | PtH attempt using planted hash |
| (Module 04) | Exported `svc.sqlreport` ticket | EAC0004 | Ticket reuse from unauthorized host |
| (Module 05) | Fake `krbtgt` hash | EAC0003 | Golden ticket forged with planted material |
| (Module 06) | Deception OU accounts | EAC0001 | DCSync targeting fake privileged accounts |
| (Module 07) | `CN=Deception_Admins` ACLs | EAC0005 | ACL enumeration/abuse on honey privileged group |
| (Module 08) | Fake LAPS password | EAC0006 | Unauthorized LAPS read from planted location |
| (Module 09) | Vulnerable template | EAC0007 | Certificate request with `Enrollee Supplies Subject` |

## Operational Notes

1. **No Alert Fatigue:** Each deception asset triggers exactly one high-fidelity rule (Level 13-14). No low-level noise.
2. **Attribution:** Source IP `::ffff:192.168.10.100` (Kali) in Event ID 4769 `IpAddress` field provides unambiguous attacker attribution.
3. **Isolation:** Deception assets are not accessible from WS-01/WS-02 during normal operations — only reachable via adversary lateral movement.
4. **Legal/Safety:** All deception occurs within isolated lab subnet (192.168.10.0/24). No production systems or real credentials involved.

## References

- MITRE Engage: https://engage.mitre.org/
- Engage Activity Matrix: https://engage.mitre.org/matrix/
- Chakravyuha Lab Architecture: `docs/architecture.md`
- Detection Catalog: `detections/README.md`
- Module 1 Purple Team Guide: `modules/01-kerberoasting/README.md`

deception.title: Deception
deception.content:
# Deception Layer

## Why

Most student AD labs are offense-only. This one treats deception as a core design element, placed before any attack runs rather than bolted on afterward — the goal isn't just catching automated tooling, but understanding what makes a decoy believable enough to fool a careful manual operator too.

That framing came out of a direct conversation with a red-team practitioner (Harpreet Singh) early in the project: deception layers are more common in mature enterprises than most self-taught offensive-security learning exposes you to (Thinkst Canary, Microsoft Defender for Identity's decoy objects, and CrowdStrike/SentinelOne's identity-protection suites all ship deception features by default). Against automated tooling it works reliably, since tooling doesn't discriminate. Against a manual operator, it comes down to engineering detail — a wrong `pwdLastSet`, a `lastLogon` that's too recent or missing entirely, an odd SPN string, any of which gives a decoy away to someone paying attention.

## What's deployed

**`svc.sqlreport`** — the lab's one honeypot account. SPN registered (`MSSQLSvc/SQLPROD01.corp.chakravyuh.local:1433`) as Kerberoasting bait, placed in the same OU as the real `svc.sqlsvc` rather than isolated in a dedicated "honey" OU — a standalone-looking "honeypot" account is itself a tell. The name was deliberately chosen to sit alongside the real `svc.sqlsvc` under the same naming convention, closer to a plausible sibling service account than a generic decoy name would be. The account was created after Module 1's initial run (2026-10-23), not before.

**Evidence:** [deception/evidence/01-wazuh-alert-100102-honeypot.json](evidence/01-wazuh-alert-100102-honeypot.json) — actual honeypot trigger alert (Rule 100102, Level 14) captured 2026-10-23.

**Canary tokens / filler bait** — two real artifacts exist:
- `IT_credentials_backup.pdf` on WS-01 desktop (`C:\Users\pnair\Desktop\IT_credentials_backup.pdf`, CreationTime 2026-07-01 12:54:45). Genuinely predates the Module 1 attack window (Sep 2026), so it was placed before the attack as the Readiness Gate requires.
- `employees.csv` on DC-01 (`C:\Users\Administrator\employees.csv`, CreationTime 2026-06-28 13:51:57). Generated via canarytokens.org and placed before the attack window. **Known limitation:** the current file on disk is plain-text CSV with a UTF-8 BOM (first byte 0xEF); no embedded callback mechanism exists in the file itself, and no companion `desktop.ini` or other folder-level canary was found. An earlier test reportedly triggered an alert, but no technical mechanism for that alert could be verified in this pass. Recommend re-generating and re-testing the token before claiming it as a verified tripwire in any blog post.

**Evidence:**
- [deception/evidence/02-employees-csv-folder-listing.png](evidence/02-employees-csv-folder-listing.png) — folder listing showing employees.csv on DC-01
- [deception/evidence/03-employees-csv-no-companion-mechanism.png](evidence/03-employees-csv-no-companion-mechanism.png) — verification of no companion mechanism (**Known limitation:** mechanism unverified)
- [deception/evidence/04-it-credentials-backup-desktop.png](evidence/04-it-credentials-backup-desktop.png) — desktop screenshot showing IT_credentials_backup.pdf on WS-01

## Design notes worth recording

**`pwdLastSet` backdating was planned but turned out to be technically infeasible** via PowerShell/LDAP — it's not a directly writable attribute in the way the original plan assumed. The actual approach: create the honeypot account early and let real elapsed time build its apparent age naturally, rather than fake a timestamp.

**Response stays passive-attribution only.** Triggering a deception object captures the triggering IP and timestamp — nothing more. Active response against a triggering system was considered and explicitly rejected; it's outside this project's scope and introduces risk disproportionate to a lab environment.

## Verification

Each deception object was manually triggered once, before Module 1 ran, to confirm it actually alerts — verifying deception after the fact (i.e., after a real attack has already happened) would defeat the purpose of having it in the first place.

hardening.title: Hardening
hardening.content:
# Hardening Philosophy

Each module in this project ends with a hardening step, but not every fix that closes an attack is actually a *fix* — some are mitigations that raise the cost of exploitation without removing the underlying weakness. This project tries to be explicit about which is which, rather than stopping at whichever fix happens to work first.

## Mitigation vs. fix — Module 1 as the worked example

Module 1 (Kerberoasting) hardened `svc.sqlsvc` in two distinct stages, applied in order:

**Stage 1 — Mitigation.** `msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes` set to `16` (AES256-only). This closes the fast, trivial version of the attack: RC4's key derivation is cheap to attack offline, AES256's is dramatically more expensive per guess. But the account's password was still human-chosen (`<redacted>` in this lab) and still guessable — AES256 makes that password slower to crack, not any less weak in principle. A well-resourced attacker with time and a decent wordlist can still get there, just more slowly.

**Stage 2 — Fix.** Migrated the real SPN to a Group Managed Service Account (`gmsa.sqlsvc`). A gMSA's password is 120 random characters, generated and auto-rotated by Active Directory itself — no human ever knows or sets it. This doesn't slow the attack down; it removes the thing the attack depends on. There's no password to guess, because no person chose one.

The distinction matters beyond this one module: a mitigation is worth applying — it's real, measurable risk reduction — but documenting it as "the fix" overstates what was actually done. Future modules in this project follow the same standard: state plainly whether a hardening step reduces risk or eliminates it, and don't claim more than what was verified.

## What "hardened" means in this project

A hardening step isn't counted as done on the strength of applying a configuration change alone. Where practical, it's followed by re-testing the original attack path to confirm the fix actually holds — for Module 1, that meant confirming `gmsa.sqlsvc`'s SPN is the only route to that service ticket now, and that `svc.sqlsvc` itself holds no SPN to target at all.

See each module's own `README.md` for its specific hardening section and verification.

sigma.content:
title: Kerberoasting from an Unrecognized Workstation Using RC4
id: 8f2c6d91-7a4e-4b3f-9c12-e5a8d0647b31
status: experimental
description: Detects Kerberos service ticket requests (Event ID 4769) using RC4 encryption (0x17) from IP addresses outside the known workstation allowlist, which may indicate Kerberoasting activity for offline service account password cracking.
author: Yash Gulati
date: 2026-10-19
references:
  - https://blog.chakravyuha.tech/post-5-kerberoasting-hardening
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1558.003

logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security

detection:
  selection_base:
    EventID: 4769

  selection_rc4:
    TicketEncryptionType: '0x17'

  filter_known_workstations:
    IpAddress:
      - '::ffff:192.168.10.30'
      - '::ffff:192.168.10.31'

  condition: selection_base and selection_rc4 and not filter_known_workstations

falsepositives:
  - Legitimate service ticket requests using RC4 from administrative systems or newly added workstations not included in the allowlist.
  - Legacy service accounts or applications that still require RC4 encryption.

level: high

    <field name="win.system.eventID">^4769$</field>
    <description>Kerberos service ticket requested (Event ID 4769) - diagnostic baseline</description>
